div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

It may safely be assumed that no part of the Royal tour in Ireland was more interesting to the King and Queen than their visit to the West. Their reception by the Connemara peasants must surely have been unique in Royal progresses, and one cannot but feel that it would have been worth going a long way to see their Majesties escorted by the Connemara horsemen and crowds of cheering peasantry. The story of the poor woman who appealed successfully to the Queen for her husband's liberty must have touched the hearts of all who read of it, and there were several other incidents of which the memory will long remain among those who witnessed them. Anyone who is seeking change of scene as well as change of air for the holidays, may safely be recommended to try Connaught, where one would be among people in every way as interesting as any that may be met with on the Continent. The Queen has not, of course, any authority to order the release of a prisoner from gaol. A London paper, in referring to the story of the poor woman who asked for the release of her husband, stated that "Her Majesty was graciously pleased to command that the remainder of the sentence should be remitted." This is investing the Queen with a power which the King him- self can only exercise through the medium of the properly constituted authorities. Moreover the infer- ence that the King and Queen are a co-existent Sovereign is entirely wrong. The King only is the Sovereign, and the Queen is just as much his Majesty's subjedt as is anyone else. Innishmicsaint lace, a specimen of which was pre, sented to Queen Alexandra, has achieved a reputation of its own in the lace making industry in the North of Ireland. It is the Irish equivalent of rose point lace, and the making of it was learnt by unravelling some old and real Venetian point. Innishmacsaint is a village in Fermanagh, and it was chiefly owing to Mrs. Maclean, the. wife of the rector of Tynan,, who provided the old point de Venise for the education of the local peasantry that it became the chief centre of the Irish rose point industry. The Queen is a great admirer of the best Irish lace, which compares favourably with any that is made in the British Isles.

The devices that have been thought out for the com- fort of bathers are many and useful, and first and fore- most. among these may be mentioned the pretty and becoming waterproof caps, which may be had at all the large shops. So many styles are now offered us, that the girl or woman who fails to find something to suit her, must indeed be difficult to please. Then there are the new straw bathing shoes, with straw soles, a great improvement upon the old varieties; and the bathing, corset, built of linen, which so many women are wear- ing this summer. Waterproof knickerbockers,volum ino us enough to accommodate skirts, petticoats, Sr.c., have been provided for the little folks, and though not elegant wear, they are garments no mother of small children should be without while sojourning at the seaside. _ _

Quite the most fashionable combination of colours is blue and pink. Needless to say great care is necessary in theselection of the two shades, but provided this is taken, the idea is a very successful one. The pink should be of the new strawberry tone that has enjoyed so wide a vogue this summer, and the blue can only be described as a light navy. In blending colours it is always well to try them by artificial as well as daylight, otherwise it may be impossible to wear a costume the whole day through. Prophetic almanacs are a little out of date, in these unsentimental times. Like the weather forecasts, they are somewhat unreliable, and no one will be greatly disturbed to learn that" Old Moore" predicts a gener- ally bad time for our country in 1904. But it was not always so, and many among the living can remember the time when prophetic almanacs were much more seri- ously regarded by the populace than they are now. There is a granddaughter of the original "Old Moore" still living at Cambridge, and she has recently presented the Queen with an !engraved portrait of the most famous of the almanac makers. His name was Henry Andrews, born in 1744, and died in 1820 and his grand- daughter Mrs. Faircloth who distinctly remembers the original seer is close upon her ninety-first year. The suggestion has been made that the churches might be used more extensively to educate the public upon worldly as well as spiritual affairs. In the Bible we are directed to the duty of caring "as well for the body as the soul," and in Canada the experiment was recently tried of handing over the churches on a given Sunday to the doctors, to enable them to discourse upon sani- tary knowledge, and its bearing upon the prevention of tuberculosis. It was thought that there is still great ignor- ance with regard to the nature and prevention of the dis- ease,and consequently this plan of educating the people from the pulpit was adopted. It has been recommended that it should be followed in our own churches, but it is to be feared that not many of the class of people most in need of sanitary enlightenment ever go to a place of worship. The solution of picture, puzzles which have long been such a prominent feature in the popular penny Press, is not, as one might imagine, a very profitable way to occupy spare time. A lady who thinks that life is suffi- ciently long to enable her to take part in these com- petitions, declares that she has received the following letter from the office of one publication.—" Dear Madame, We regret that, owing to the unprecedented number of successful competitors, the amount available for each person is only lid. Deducting a penny for postage,that leaves one halfpenny, which we enclose. Please acknow- ledge receipt." Probably not many of the competitors comply with the last request, but even if that is so, the Post Office seems to be the only institution that profits from these competitions. Chess problems are now a common feature in the daily and weekly Press, but it is not generally known, that many of these are the work of Mrs. W. J. Baird who lives at Brighton. Mrs. Baird is a living example of the doctrine of hereditary talent as both her parents were ardent chess players; and problem composers and other members of her family, are also well-known in chess circles. She was quite an infant prodigy in the solution of Chinese puzzles, and she could easily solve the most difficult of these when she was but four years of age, and with her parents training shejsoon developed extraordinary skill in the intricate game of chess. Pro- bably no other game offers such infinite opportunities of variety of position, but some of the most famous chess problems have been composed by Mrs. Baird, and many of them have been published all the world over. MAD GE.

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

Holiday garb and what is best to take with us to the seaside or the country occupies muoh of our thoughts just now, but the wisest plan is to let common . sense prevail, and take only such things as are actually necessary. Blouses of various degrees of smartness, together with a couple of skirts, one plain and preferably of navy blue serge cut to clear the ground all round, and the other of voile or some such light material knife pleated or trimmed with lace, together with a plain flat French sailor hat and one of a more dressy mode, will be .found quite sufficient for a short visit. The addition of a couple of washing cotton frocks and one

div.head: ,PRETTY COST
div.p: A ,PRETTY COST

of lace - trimmed muslin Fill suffice for any length of time, provided he services of a decent laundress are obtainable. In choosing ready-made coats and skirts it is always ad- visable to select those that are pleated, for skirts that are box-pleated, knife-pleated, and soleil-plissé will be popular for some time to come. The length of these should be what is now known as the trottoir skirt, which clears the ground all round. ,It de- pends altogether on the figure of the wearer' whether the pleats are left loose or stitched down for some inches below the line of the waist, but in no instance should the stitch- ing extend very far, for there must not be permitted any suspicion of tightness near the knees. The pretty costume sketched is of pale green voile, both the bolero and skirt being pleated. The bolero, which is made something after the fashion of a sailor blouse (and is accordion pleated from collar to waist) is drawn in a few inches above the waist line by a narrow ribbon threaded in and out of the material, which is finished at the waist by a band of folded silk. The col-
LINEN BLOUSE B

lar is of handsome embroidery. The plissé bolero will certainly remain as long in favour as the pleated skirt, but it is nowadays always cut sufficiently short to show a con- siderable amount of the waist band worn beneath it. Shot or chine taffetas make up also into fascinating little sac visites, and do not require much trimming, a little sia-A lace ruching round the collar, fronts and cuffs or some lace appliqué in the form of motifs proving quite_ sufficient. These pretty little coats are quite within the powers of the home dressmaker, as there is not any very great accuracy of fit required. Many of the most modish linen frocks are made with a kilted or pleated bolero, but the blouse bodice seems more appropriate and looks exceedingly well drawn into a deep waistband. The blouse bodice illustrated is very simply made with a lace yoke continued down the front, while the fulness is confined by the deep waistband. Sometimes these bodices are further enhanced by a Louis XIII. col- lar of lace or by a Marie Antoinette fichu, a dainty chemisette of fine lace filling up the opening at the throat. Some of the newest large lace collars are edged by a silk ruching or a shaded silk fringe, and more attention
than ever is given to their fit on the shoul- ders.

A more elaborate finish to a deep collar which really arrived at the dimensions of a cape consisted of an edging of short strands of coloured narrow ribbon each finished by a gilt or enamelled ornament. , Those of my readers who are meditating a sojourn by the seaside should bear in mind in selecting bath hats and gowns that all delicate colours should be avoided. Indeed, it is wisest to have as little colour as possible in our toilettes, and to wear the tussore or holland shades which are so fashionable this season. These do not fade, and will wash well, while the addition of a pretty-coloured cravat and waistband will smarten them up considerably. Flowers will be found a highly unsatisfactory trimming for ,hats, as the salt sea air soon takes all the colour out. Rib- bons will prove much more serviceable, and should always be selected in preference to flowers or foliage. Bathing costumes are vastly different nowadays from the hideous blue serge gar- ments of yore which had not the faintest pretensions to any sort of shape, and ren- dered the wearer unsightly however liberally endowed by nature With a graceful figure. A smart bathing dress is given in my illus- tration, which, though simple, is neat, and allows the wearer thereof plenty of freedom in the water. Nowadays when nearly every girl swims the question of weight has to be considered, for some materials become very heavy when wet, and would seriously impede the movements of the wearer in the water. Navy blue or scarlet are the best colours • for bathing costumes, although some more dar- ing individuals adopt stripes or pale colours. such as pink or blued These latter, how. ever, soon fade and look uglyd CoguErrni

THE
BY HARRIS BURLAND. AUTHOR or"DAcoaßrCrre.
CHAPTER XI 11. —Continued.

It was a great fight, but it was over in less than five minutes. Tredegar was over- powered by numbers and bound hand and foot. His face and hands were red with blood .and he trembled in every limb. Then he looked at the crowd 'and smiled. He had marked a dozen of them, and four had broken limbs. It was a great fight, he thought to himself, one worthy of -Samson and the Philistines.
Three figures had stood apart from the combat, two men and a woman. They now approached. Walroyd came forward to meet them with a lantern in his hand. As he saw the woman's face he started.
"You, Miss Cantrip," .he cried in amaze- ment, "What
"We were only just in time to save her,", her father broke in.

" Ah. the scream," said Walroycl. "I thought it sounded like a woman, but we could not see from this side. Well, he's safe enough now. I am glad we did come in time. Yet how on earth did you come here, Miss Cantrip." _ _
For a Moment she hesitated. Then she saw that she was bound to continue the lie.

"I fell asleep round by .the rocks this after- noon," she said faintly. "When I woke, it was getting dark, and I was cut off from Garth by the tide. So I had to come along this way. Then a man grasped me by the arm. I did not see his face, but I was frightened and screamed. That is all." " The scoundrel," said Mr. Morgan," thank God we have got him. He'll swing now." "Let's look at him," said Mr. Cantrip, swinging his lantern and peering to where Tredegar stood surrounded by his captors. "A strong fellow, eh I Done some damage, eh! Yet I wager I once saw a man who could have downed him, eh!' Cynthia? I should like to look at hirh. You'd better stay here, my girl, with Mr. Walroyd," and he blinked his little eyes as he saw a flush of pleasure cross the American's face. For John Walroyd was never insensible to the beauty of a woman,. and Mr. Cantrip had more than once during the past fortnight noticed the, American's admiration for his daughter. "No, I will come with you," she .answered firmly. An idea had ,flashed across her brain. She had yet another part to play in this tragedy. "You had better stay here," Mr. Cantrip answered coldly. "This is no sight for a woman," and he moved towards the crowd. She turned her back on Walroyd and followed. The latter bit his lips' with vexation, and then walked slowly after her.
As they neared the group of men they saw by the light of the lanterns that several of them were. hurt, and that four were stretched out on the ground. The old, man chuckled.

"By the -Gods," he said, "a pretty fight, a pretty fight. Where is he ? I should like to see him.' The crowd opened out 'and they pushed Tredegar a little forward, forgetting that his feet were bound. He fell forward with a crash. Cynthia's 'face whitened and a look of fury shot from her eyes. The men laughed, and. half a dozen of them hauled Tredegar to his feet again and set him up, as one sets up a fallen pillar. His forehead was streaked and stained with blood, and it tritkled down his dirty unshaven cheeks. The -old man came close to him, and raising the lantern, peered up into the ghastly face. He started, and a keen 'observer might have noticed that the hand which held the lantern trembled. Then his daughter who was behind him suddenly sprang forward with, a cry of surprise, and snatching the lantern from his hand held it up within a foot of Tredegar's face.

"Father," she cried, "who is this ?- Surely there is some mistake. This is Mr. Edwards, the man who was ill at,our house. Don't you remember him ? There is some awful mis- take here. Why, at the very time .the second murder was committed this man was ill. I read the account of it to him myself from the newspaper," and .she turned round and faced the crowd that . was pressing close to her to hear her words. Mr. Cantrip ,looked sharply up at her excited face, and in a flash he read the whole truth. His daughter had come- to the beach that night to meet Emrys .Tredegar, to warn him of his danger, to. He blazed with fury, but restrained himself, and pre- tended to closely scrutinize the young giant's face.

"Well, Mr. Cantrip," said Tredegar coldly. "Do you know me ? " "Yes," the old man answered, "I recog- nise you. Your name was then Edwards. You doubtless changed, it for an excellent reason. I did not know we were entertaining a. murderer.
"But, father," the daughter cried eagerly, "he could not have committed the second murder. He was with

"I think your memory plays you false," the old man said quietly. " I distinctly re- member reading of the second murder five (lays after he left ,us. You are distracted with all you have gne -through, Cynthia. We will go home," and turning away from Tredeaar he began to rtiove across the shingle with feeble steps. For a moment Cynthia Cantrip stood look- ing at his retreating figure with scorn and loathing in her eyes. Then she saw that Walroyd was keenly watching the expression of her face and she laughed nervously. ." Yes, I think I will go home," she said in a calm voice, and then swayed as though she would have fallen. However, she quickly recovered herself, and tooked once more at • Tredegar. "Come along," said her father roughly. "Mr. Walroyd, can we go back in one of the boats. I am an old man, and I don't think I can manage the walk to-night. I. daresay ico'ou can find room for IN." "Certainly," replied Walroyd abstractedly, still keeping his eves on Miss Cantrip's face. "We have to take Tredegar by boat. But perhaps you would not care to go in that one."

• " Oh, yes," the old man said with an evil smile. "We will certainly go in that one if you are in it. We shall be quite safe." Cynthia Cantrip clenched, her hands. •" Safe," .she said to herself; "Aye, if Emrys Tredegar could, but be free for a ,moment, you would be safe." Th.pnishe felt in her pocket for a small knife she usually carried there.
"Perhaps," Walroyd said, "Miss Cantrip would not care to---"
"Thank you, Mr. Walroyd," she broke in, "1 do not mind *ho is in the boat."

Walroyd left them and gave orders to the men. The wounded were carefully lifted up and laid in one of the boats. Half a dozen sailors got in with them, and then another half dozen ran the craft off the shingle, and leapt into it, as it went gliding from the shore. Then another batcla, picked up Tredegar and placed him in the Second boat. Walro,fl, Miss Morgan, Mr. Cantrip, and his daughter took their places, and no one noticed that the latter skilfully contrived to be near the prisoner. Then the boat was launched and headed towards Garth. Th.; remainder had to return, by the cliffs;' And looking ,back, Trede- gar saw the waving line of yellow lights mov- ing along the shore, and heard the, strain of a Welsh hymn sung by the sailors. He could scarcely resist• a smile, as the harmonies came across the water to his ears.' There was little light • from the sky overhead and only a single lantern flickered in the 'bow of the boat. Cynthia drew out her small pen- knife and felt cautiously for the cords that bound Tredegar's feet. Then a thrill , of horror ran thrcit:2,ll her, for she encountered
the cold touch of steel. They had substituted manacles and handcuffs for the cords with

they had first bound him: She shut up the knife and replacing it in her pocket clasped her hands in silent agony. In half an hour they reached Garth. Long before they touched the shore they could see a dense crowd of people, and the continuous moving of lights along the beach. When they were fifty yards from the ripples at the edge, a chorus of voices greeted them.
Have you got him? Have you seen him ?" •

" Aye, aye," the answer came back from the sailors in the boat. "We have him right enough." Then they landed, and lifted Tredegar on to the beach. A dense crowd swayed round his prostrate form, and the air rang. with shouts and jokes. "You curs !" he said, quietly. "Lift me to my feet." They seized hold of him and set him up- right. Then he suddenly snarled like a wild beast, and lifted his manacled hands above his head, and the crowd shrank back. The chains clinked on his trembling wrists, and murder was in his soul: A single blow from the irons on his hands wciuld have dashed out a man's brains. -

All at once there was a stir in the crowd, and a woman forced her way through them to Tredegar's side. It was Mavanwy I As he saw her, all the lust of blood died out of his heart, and his great hands sank down before him.

Then, without shame or hesitation, she threw her arms round his neck, and kissed him, and when she had moved her lips from his her face was stained with blood. Then 3he turned on the crowd, and tried to speak, but the words would not come, and she sank senseless to the ground. The crowd stood in silence. But far on the edge of it, almost where the waves rippled to the shore, another woman buried her head in her hands and wept bitterly.

div.head: CHAPTER XIV.
div.p: CHAPTER XIV.
THE SACRIFICE.

THERE was no prison cell in the little vil- lage of Garth, and the back parlour of the policeman's house generally served for the trivial offenders that brought themselves within reach of the law. It was felt, how- ever, that a man of such gigantic strength and ferocity as Tredegar, arrested, moreover, on so serious a charge as murder, required a more secure confinement than the four walls of an ordinary room. Walroyd suggested- one of the cellars of the Plas Tredegar, and the idea was eagerly seized on by the more brutal of the crowd. It amused their coarse natures to think of a man being locked 'up in his own house: The two policemen were 'gore impressed by the facts which Walroyd • put before them— namely, that the cellars were without win- dows, that the walls were part of the solid rock itself, and that the doors were made of six inches of oak, clamped with iron, and furnished with modern Bramah locks.

Morgan and Walroyd—the latter of whom was an Englishrtian, in spite -of the many years he had spent in America—were both Justices of the Peace, and after a brief consultation they ,ordered the prisoner to be taken up to the Plas Tredegar for the night, and to be removed to the County gaol on the following day. Several men placed Tredegar on a cart, and set off 'slowly dowii the village. Walroyd then insisted on both the Morgans and the Cantrips coming home with him to spend the night, giving, as the reason for the invitation that Miss. Morgan was too ill to stand the long drive to Llynglas, and that Miss Cantrip would be required to keep her company. Both the fathers acquiesced willingly in the suggestion; Mr. Morgan, because his (laughter was still faint and weak, and it would be impossible to take her back to Llynglas that night, and Mr. Cantrip because he saw the way Walroyd had looked at Cynthia as he issued the invitation, and guessed that the American was seeking some opportunity of seeing his daughter alone. Mavanwy was too ill to offer any opposition and Cynthia, for her own reasons, was silent. She was working out ,a plan in her subtle brain, and the invitation supplied the one link she 'required to join the various parts into a perfect whole. They got into Walroyd's waggonette, which was waiting in the street, and calling at the Cantrips' lodgings for the few things necessary for the' night, drove rapidly down the long street. At the foot of the hill they passed the slow procession taking Emrys to his prison. Cyn- thia looked back on it with tightened lips. Dilavanwy sat with closed eyes and saw nothing. The -three men smiled grimly at eath other.

• When they reached the house they all had supper, and directly. afterwards Mavanwy went up todbed. It had been arranged that Cynthia should sleep in the same room with her, and though the latter now loathed the very sight of her rival, she could not with decency refuse this little comfort to the sick girl. When Mavanwy had left the room, Wal- rovd touched the bell.
- _ . _ " Send one of the policemen here," he said, when the. footman entered.
The man returned, and in a few minutes afterwards the heavy step of P.C. Davies, the village constable, was heard outside, and there was a loud knocking at the door, " Come in!" cried Walroyd. .
The door opened, and a large, grizzly- bearded man stood sheepishly in the entrance. "Well, Davies," said Walroyd, "how. -is the prisoner ?"
"Quiet, sir, aye, indee(l., very quiet."
_ Walroyd laughed. "What do you think of the prison, Davies ?"
"Very strong, sir, and not too comfort- able. We've given him some straw to lie 0n.,,
-" I'll come down and look," Walrovd said. "Perhaps you had better Come, too, Mr. Morgan, and you, Mr. Cantrip. I am sure Miss Cantrip will excuse us." . She smiled sweetly.

"I think I will 'come with you," she said. " I am afraid of being left alone." And she gave Walroyd a warm glance of affection that made him tremble and wish that he could stay behind with her and gel rid of the old men.

"Very well," he replied. "We will all go I am sure Tredegar ought to.be flattered." They made their way through several long corridors, and then down a flight of stone steps. At the bottom of these there was another passage, terminating in a heavy door. The policeman went on in front with a lantern; Walroyd and Cynthia brought up the rear. ,Under cover of the darkness she laid her hand upon his arm, and a thrill went through hi. Whole body. He raised the hand to his lips and kissed it silently. She did not resist.

The party stopped on the threshold, and P.C. Davies unlo'cked the door and, entering the_ cellar, cast the light of the lantern round the walls, so that they could see everything. It was a cold, dreary spot to spend the night in. Floor and ceiling were both of stone, and , the walls seemed to have been planed out from the solid rock. A few wine-bins ran along on one side, but they were empty. A heap of straw had been thrown in the centre of the floor, and Tredegar lay on this; with his face buried iii his arms.
"Has he had food and water, constable ?" queried Walroyd. `` Yes, sir. We fed..hirii like a baby. Daren't
free his hands." At the sound of _ the voice, Tredegar raised

himself, and the chains rattled on his limbs. He blinked as the yellow light shone into his eyes, and tried to peer into the darkness beyond. He was a pitiable sight to look upon. His hair was caked and matted with blood his eyes blazed like -two live coals. He showed his teeth through his half-open lips like some- wild beast. Then, for a brief second, the light from Davies' lantern fell on the little group by the door. He saw the faces of the three men, and behind them, almost in the shadow, the red-gold light of. a woman's hair. He tried to rise to his feet, but 'only succeeded in struggling to' his knees, and. his chains clanked heavily as he shook his great arms towards the door. "Leave me," he cried, "or by God, I will come closer to you than you care for," and he shuffled along on his knees towards them, Davies sprang forward, and seizing him by the shoulders, linrled him off his balance on to the straw. Cynthia's hands clenched so tightly that the nails drew blood from her soft white palms. Tredegar lay quite still, and Davies backed cautiously towards the door. "Excited, eh ! " said Walroyd. "I think we will close this interview!' When they were all qutside he shut the door, and taking the key from the constable, turned it in the lock. In the old days a heavy mass of iron would have accomplished this task, but Walroyd had had 'patent locks pit in all over the house. Then they returned to the smoking room, and again in the passage Cynthia's hand con- trived to touch Walroyd's. He grasped it 'fervently in his strong fingers, and then tried to place his arm about,her waist. But she moved.. a little away from him. When they emerged into the light, their eyes met, and she blushed and looked away from him. He burned with passion and longed to clasp her is his arms. The men finished their cigars, and then Cynthia and her father and Mr. Morgan went up to bed. Walroyd remained behind, He had, so he said, certain matters of business to go into, and certain accounts to make out before -the morning. He lit a fresh cigar, and going over tO his desk, pulled out a mass of papers and began to sort them. Cynthia looked back at him as she left the room and smiled. He had squeezed her hand very tenderly as he said good-night. She went up to her room, and closing the door, walked over to the bed where Mavanwy lay asleep. The girl's dark hair flowed in rippling waves over the pillow. Her face was white, and her lips parted. She stirred uneasily in her sleep. Cynthia looked at her careworn and beautiful, face, and then walk- ing over to the cheval glass, gazed for a minute at her own self. Then, returning to the bed, she, looked again at the sleeping form, as though comparing notes with what she had seen in the glass, and her face grew hard and bitter as she looked. " You are younger," she said softly as though addressing the sleeping girl, but you do not love him more, and you are not more pleasing to look upon, and you would not do more to save him.' Then she turned out the light, and opening the door, quietly made her way back to the smoking room. The house was wrapt in silence, and even her soft footfalls on the velvet pile carpet seemed to sound alarmingly. She opened the door, and then drew back as she saw the light still burning inside. "Who is there," said Walroyd, quickly shuffling some papers over a glittering object that lay on the desk before him. Cynthia held the door half open, but did not show herself. "I'm so' sorry, -Mr. Walroyd," she said softly; "but Mavanwy left her smelling salts somewhere about, and she wants them. sCould you give them to me." Walroyd pretended to look about the room. The salts were on a small table close to where Mavanwy had been sitting. He glanced at them with a smile, and put them in his pocket, but continued to search somewhat ostenta- tiously. "I can't see them," he said in a tone of vexation. "Will you come in and look for " yourself." She opened the door a little wider and stood irresolutely in the doorway, as though half afraid to enter. Walroyd looked round from the corner where he was searching diligently and his face flushed. Rarely had he set eyes on so glorious a vision as the one he gazed upon. The white beautiful face, the crown of copper hair, the diamonds flashing on her hands and throat, and something inde- finable that he had not seen before—a look of passion in the violet eye% a faint glow on the cheeks, like the flush Of coming dawn, the slight parting of the lips that almost seemed to tremble with expectation. Walroyd ad- vanced a step or two across the room. "Please come in, Miss Cantrip," he said. "You needn't be afraid." She laughed nervously, and entering the room, began to look round for the bottle of

salts. It was needless to say that she did not find it. Walroyd chuckled to himself. He did not know that she had mapped out the whole game, and was going to play it to the end. Then, as they were both searching among some odds and ends on a table, their hands chanced to touch, and Walroyd seized her cold white fingers in a warm clasp. She tried feebly to withdraw them, and then laughed. Please, Mr. Walroyd' she said, "I can't look for anything if you do that." He seized her other hand and raised both to his lips: Then he drew her close to him, and loosing her hands, clasped her in his arms, and kissed her passionately. "Cynthia," he cried hoarsely, "I love yon. My darling, I love you." A shudder of loathing passed through . her body, and she could hardly restrain herself from crying out in horror. Then she burst into tears, and he let go of her. Cynthia," he continued eagerly, "I have not offended you. I could not help it. I love you so much. Will you be my wife ? " "Your wife I " she said slowly, "your wife ? " She had not dreamt of this. She had hoped to gain her point with a few kisses. But his wife—that would. be too horrible a sacrifice. # "I do not love you, Mr. Walroyd," she said simply. "I will make you love me," he answered passionately. "I am rich and can give you all you ask for. You love jewels, do you not ? " and he glanced at the gems sparkling on her fingers. "See here." He strode over to a steel safe let into the wall, opened it, attd taking out a box, poured its contents on to a velvet cushion. Every gem of the earth was there, and the heap sparkled with every colour of the rainbow. Her eyes glistened, and she turned the jewels over with trem- bling hands. For the moment she forgot even-Emrys Tredegar. "These are mine," he said, "and more a hundredfold. Your father is selling off my collection. Perhaps you have seen some of them." Her mind went back to the dingy parlour in River Street, and then by the association of ideas to Enirys Tredegar. She turned her back on the glittering heap and was silent. Walroyd Came close to her and tried once more to take her. hand. She moved away from him. " I must think," she said in a low voice. " Please let me think." For two minutes neither of them spoke. Walroyd busied himself with replacing the jewels in the box, and Cynthia stood with her eyes fixed, on the window, as motionless as though she had, been turned to stone. At last she made .up her mind, and turned her beautiful 'face to Walroyd. "I will marry you, .Mr. Walroyd," she said slowly. "but only on one condition. 1 want von to give me something." "Name it," he said, striding towards her. " If it is in my gift, you shall have it." " I want," she continued, "the key of the cellar in which Mr. Tredegar is confined. .vant also a key to the handcuffs and manacles. Mr. Tredegar must go free to-night. These ure my terms." • To be continued.)

div.head: EVENTS OF THE WEEK
div.p: EVENTS OF THE WEEK
THE KING'S RETURN.

It was very fortunate that the King man- aged to return from Ireland at a holiday time, enabling hundreds of workers to get a glimpse of the Victoria and Albert, if not o its royal passengers. The yacht came to Cowes, and right hearty was the reception accorded it. Great numbers of excursionists made this pretty little Isle of Wight town their resort for the day, while a larger num- ber, going to Southampton, Gosisort, or Ports- mouth, collected on the south shore of the mainland to catch a glimpse of the trim royal craft as she came up the Solent. Cowes, at all times displaying a charming front, looked more picturesque than ever on Monday with
THE ARRIVAL OF THE VICTORIA AND ALBERT YACHT OFF COWES. TAKEN FROM PRINCE'S GREEN.

its liberal decorations. Cowes is famous the world over for its regatta, but if its charms were more widely known it would be equally famous as a watering place. As it is, how- ever, its charms are not very gene/ally known, and holiday makers to the Garden of England rush to towns with more widely chronicled virtues. There is at Cowes an unrivalled parade, from which there is a magnificent view across the Solent, especially when the roadstead is crowded with yachts and boats, and launches arc darting in all directions. In a prominent position at the entrance to the harbour is the new Victoria Pier, where the excursion steamers now usually, land their passengers instead of at the pontoon. With this addition to its conveni- ences Cowes is likely to become the most popular resort in the island for lovers of the sea. At Cowes also is the famous Castle, the headquarters of the world - renowned Royal Yacht Squadron. This is the premier yacht club of thc kingdom, having for many years had the King, as Prince of Wales, as its com- modore, and now as its admiral, the German Emperor as member, patron, and annual prize-giver, and a membership list including half the British aristocracy.

div.head: NAVAL MANCEUVRES.
div.p: THE NAVAL MANCEUVRES.

The sham naval war which has been in pro- gress this week is one of exceptional interest inasmuch as the fleets are the largest and most powerful that have ever been afloat in warfare—mimic or otherwise. The object, of course, is a. trial of strength and skill, both on the offensive and defensive sides, and for this reason none of the defenders knew pre cisely what he had to meet, and when and where the attack was to be ex- pected. At the commencement, on the one side was the Mediterranean squadron under Admiral Sir Compton Domvile, and that

CHARLES BERESFORD. ADMIRAL WILSON. ADMIRAL SIR C. DOMVILB. known for manceuvre purposes as the X fleet was at Gibraltar. Pitted against it were the Channel and reserve squadrons, under Admiral Wilson and Lord Charles Beresford, and these were known as fleets B i and B 2. While the big ships were racing about the Atlantic. from Belfast to Madeira, there was a highly interesting set of torpedo-craft manceuvres in the Irish Channel. No fewer than ninety-eight craft were engaged—sixty-one destroyers and thirty-seven torpedo boats—and a few old battleships, irreverently dubbed "bumboats " by the sailors, lay in harbour as bases for the flotillas. The Blue Fleet was on the Irish side of the Channel, the Red Fleet on the English. Their bases were as far apart as Belfast and Queenstown on the one side, and Holyhead and the Scilly Islands on the other. Each English flotilla faced an opposing flotilla on the Irish coast, so that, for once, at any rate, England has been at war against Ireland during the 20th century. The weight and power of the ships in the two sets of manoeuvres may be seen from the following list: 32 battle- ships, including three old ones for torpedo operations; 8 armoured cruisers, one of an old. type; 7 ist class protected cruisers; 24 znd class; 9 3rd class; 13 torpedo gun- boats; 61 torpedo-boat destroyers, and 37 torpedo-boats. In the whole of the German navy there are only twenty-three battleships and twenty-eight cruisers.

div.head: P. AND O.'S LATEST.
div.p: THE P. AND O.'S LATEST.

On Saturday last a new type of vessel started upon her maiden voyage, and her career will be watched with no small interest. This was the Peninsular and Oriento steamer Palermo, the pioneer of a class of large screw steamers which are to be primarily adapted for cargo, Whilst carrying a small complement of passengers. Therefore her holds are very large and clear in order to facilitate stowage, and she is fitted on the new system with a large number of cranes and derricks so that she may be expeditiously loaded and unladen.

THE PALERMO, THE FIRST OF , THE NEW CLASS. In all the arrangements for dealing with cargo consist of ten steam cr.a.nes and five derricks, one of which by itself is capable of lifting thirty tons! Everything is of the most com- plete description, and the Palermo is fitted with two sets of triple expansion engines and two large double-ended boilers. In length she is 496 feet, in beam 57 ft. 3 in., and in depth 35 ft. 9 in. The accommodation for passen- gers and officers is under the bridge. The Palermo has been built by Messrs. Barclay, Curie & Co., of Whiteinch, Glasgow. She pro-. raises to prove a most useful boat, and marks an era of progress in British mercantile ship. Ping 4

div.head: SCULPTURAL TRIUMPH.
div.p: A SCULPTURAL TRIUMPH.

The royal tour which has just been con. eluded promises, to leave a permanent mark Irish politics, as it has gone far to clear uf misunderstandirtgs which previously existed or were supposed to existe. Before its com- mencement there were rumours of disloyalty on all sides, but eyerythiug has gone to dis- prove these ill-conditioned canards, and in no part of the country have the King and Queen met with such an uproarious or enthusiastic welcome since their accession as in the Emerald Isle. Of it they can only carry away happy recollections and goldeh opinions, such as exist of themselves in the hearts of the Irish. They are a warm-hearted race, and probably the most telling of their grievances have been the long periods of royal absence in the past, which are now, however, never again likely to occur. A royal Court in Dublin promises now to become a regular part of the ceremori'll order cf the year, and it will be a source of keen joy an delight to the loyal Irish. Dublin, despite certain ill-condi- tioned efforts prior to the tour to upset the
THE NEW VICTORIA MONUMENT,

div.head: BELFAST,
div.p: BELFAST,

harmony of the proceedings, was enthusi- astically loyal to a man, and Belfast seemed to be anxious to out-rival the capital, when the King and Queen visted it at the close of their stay with the Marquis and Marchioness of Londonderry at Mount Stewart. The town turned out en masse, and their Majesties had a right royal reception all along the route. The chief business of the day was the un- veiling of the monument to the late Queen— a statue of Queen Victoria by Mr. Brock, R.A„ which stands just opposite the Town Hall. This function was performed by the King, who was presented with a silver replica. This was followed by a public luncheon in the Town Hall, after which the King and Queen formally opened the Victoria Hospital. Later in the afternoon they trained to Bangor and embarked on the royal yacht. The rest of the week was spent in cruising round the coast and making excursions into the interior. The final scene was the visit to Cork end its ex- hibition ;on Saturday, which concluded the royal programme. From Ireland the royal yacht steamed to Cowes.

div.head: LONDON'S NEW FIRE CHIEF.
div.p: LONDON'S NEW FIRE CHIEF.

Considerable discussion has been aroused upon all sides by the choice of Captain Wells' successor at the head of the London Fire Bri- gade. Probably of all the candidates the public 'favourite was Mr. Gamble, the existing second in command, but the Fire Brigade and General Pu r- poses Commit-

of six naval and military officers.

However, in Dr. Cooper the cause of "promotion from the ranks" did not find a very able or impressive advocate. He was followed by Mr. Steadman, a Labour representative, who spoke in a fiery and exaggerated strain. He, however, was entirely squelched by an effective speech from his colleague. Mr. John Burns, who is always actuated by sound common sense. He, he said, had no prejudice in the matter, and was only anxious to see the best man appointed, "be he a down-at-heel aristocrat or an unduly elated Labour leader." The applicants from the provinces had nect come up to sample; and he expressed it as his .opinion that of the thirty-five candidates Captain Hamilton was the best. Thus the amendment was lost, and Captain Hamilton was duly appointed suc- cessor to Captain Wells. Thus another naval officer becomes Chief of the London Fire Brigade.

div.head: NOTEWORTHY FIRE BRIGADE ADDITION.
div.p: A NOTEWORTHY FIRE BRIGADE ADDITION.

In all the varied spheres of to-day where to lc get there first" is the supreme law, there is none in which the words have such meaning as in the fire brigade. Remarkable inventive activity has been displayed quite recently in fire-extinguishing improvements, and ingenuity cciuld hardly be better applied. The most recent innovation that is on trial in London is the first-aid motor. This marks a really important forward step in the fire-extinguish- ing problem. In appearance this new engine is very much like an • ordinary motor car. Captain Wells is very enthusiastic about it, and gave an appreciative description of it at the annual fire brigade display. When in general use, he said, it would be despatched to

a 'fire immediately on a call being received. It would outstrip either escape or engine, and on arriving at a fire, being equipped with ladders, would facilitate rescue work, and carrying its own supply of water in a tank, the extinction of • the fire would commence before the larger engines could connect up and begin pumping. The water it carries is chemi- cally impregnated, and, ff many cases, the probability is that it will have effected the extinction of the flames before the bigger engines come up. As it greatly outstrips in pace bOth horse fire escapes and ordinary fire engines, its value will be at once apparent, for the saving of a few minutes between a call and the brigade arrival often makes all the difference between a big fire and a little one z-

HIS DEFINITION.--" What is a flirt?" asked the small boy. "A flirt," replied the old bachelor, "is a pretty woman." "But what kind of a pretty woman 1" persisted the small boy. "Any kind of a pretty woman," answered the old bachelor. "Well, how pretty must she be?" the youngster insisted. "Oh, pretty enough to have a chance to flirt," returned the old bachelor, irritably. "Only a couple of days, but I saw everything worth seeing.' She: " Really ! Then you saw the lion ot St. Mark's, I suppose?" He: " Rathec ! Saw him fed." (And the conversation flagged) "MAY I ask, ma'am," said the new boarder, "if this is imitation coffee?" "And may I ask why you ask?" queried the imperturbable land- lady. "Because real coffee, ma'am, keeps me awake nights." "By the exercise of a little patience, then," said the smiling landlady, "you will soon be able to answer the question for your. ? Won't you have another cup?" ARE you the society editor?" asked the large lady, who seemed to fill the room. "No, madam," said the one addressed. "1 am only the Court re- porter." " Really !I am surprised. But, perhaps you will do. Your paper said in its account of the affair at my house that floral decorations lent beauty to the scene.' I wish you would have your paper state that the floral beauty was not lent. Everything was paid for." His sister wished to discourage him, but was anxious to do it in a quiet way that would not make trouble—so she said: "Bow old is she?" was asked. " ehe says she is 18," he replied. "Well," she returned, "the next time you go to see her you'd better take along an almanac. She evidently has forgotten how to reckon time." When it comes to breaking things gently there is no one who is quite so successful as a.disgasted woman.

WHEN Mr. A. J. Balfour was Chief Secretary of Ireland, he one day came across a daughter of Erin digging up her patch of potatoes, and he remarktd on their quality. " Ah, bad luck to Mr. Balfour! I wish I could see him!" said the woman. "The seeds he gave us were no good." "I'm Mr. Balfour." She gazed hard, and after a chat with him, then exclaimed: "Sure, now, haven't I often heard that the devil's not so black as he's painted " A PLEASANT TIME.—" Now then, my dear," said Mr. Binks, as he placed his camera in position, compose yourself and let a pleasant thought pass through your mind." "Nice. time to expect a woman . to have pleasant thoughts, isn't it?" exclaimed Mrs. Binks. "The boiler sprung a leak, tho fire gone out, the bread settled flat as a pancake, DO firewood, pump won't pump a drop, baby's got a pain, the twins to dress for school, music-teacher coming to give Emmeline her lesson, washerwoman soon be here, I should be at the station this moment to meet mother, have just an hour left before I'm due at the morning session to deliver my leekure before the Good Housekeeper's Club on the subject of How to Manage a Kitchen'; yes, it's a nice time for a pleasant thought to pass through a woman's mind. ONLY A RECRUIT, BUT A. DEAD SE/OT.—A good story is told at the expense of a lieutenant who was drilling recruits in revolver practice. One of the recruits was a tall and ungainly fellow from a mountain district. The monntaineer was shown how to load, hold, and handle his pistol by the dapper young officer, and after many corrections by the officer finally struck the right way to hold the revolver. "is that right?" he asked, at last. "All right," responded the lieutenant. "Now see if you can fire without killing any of our men." Rip ! went the revolver, pointing towards a target one hundred yards distant. Ping, ping, ping! went the bullets until the six-shooter was empty. The target was brought in, and there were six clear bull's-eyes. "Is that right ? " asked the raw-boned Southerner. The lieutenant did not say a word, and the camp has been laughing ever since.

WHO SHE WAS - The following story of a famous doctor is not a new one, but the point is a good one, though the dootor's speech was blunt. Dr. Jephsen, an English physician of former repu- tation like Dr. Abernethy, won his fame partly by his bluntness. One day he was called to the Duchess of Marlborough, who told him of all her symptoms at great length. Ris advice was: "One egg and one cup ot tea for breakfast; then a walk ; a piece of cold roast beef for luncheon; then a walk; a good cutlet for dinner; then another walk, and then to bed. No carriage riding." "You seem to forget who and what I am ' said the duchess. "Not at all," replied Dr. Jephsen. "You are an old woman with a ruined stomach !"

div.head: MUNICIPAL TRADING. The Alleged Irregularities at Stockport.
div.p: MUNICIPAL TRADING. The Alleged Irregularities at Stockport.
Proposed Inquiry.

The recent disclosures in connection with the cleans- ing department of the Stockport Corporation are still agitating the public mind at Stockport, and there is a strong feeling that an independent inquiry into the management of a department should be held. The Cleansing Committee recently passed a number of resolutions as to the conduct of certain officials, but it is felt that there ougiht to be a thorough investigation into the affairs of the department, and Councillor Briggs has given notice that he will moveat the Council meeting the following resolution That having re- gard to the recent disclosures of irregularities in the management of the cleansing department it is impera- tive in the interest of the town that there should be a. public inquiry, and that a select committee be appoint- ed from the members of the Council (other than those on the Cleansing Committee) to make such investigation and to report to the Council."

div.head: Report of the Parliamentary Joint Committee.
div.p: Report of the Parliamentary Joint Committee.

The report from the Joint Selectrommittee of the House!of Lords and the House of Commons on Municipal Trading, with the proceedings of the committee, was issued on Wednesday afternoon as a Parliamentary paper The committee felt that any attempt to survey the general subject of municipal trading could only have led to a second postponement of the inquiry. They agreed therefore, to devote their attention to one or more dis- tinct aspects of the question. The first branch of the subject with which the committee decided to deal was that of municipal accounts. The report states that, whatever view may be taken of the proper limits, if any, which can be set to municipal trading, it is clearly important that wherever it exists the ratepayers should be not less fully and continuously informed of the success or failure of each undertaking than if they were shareholders in an ordinary trading company. In a large number of cases this is undoubt- edly done. But there is in some instances evidence to a contrary effect, and, in view of the ever-increasing number and magnitude of municipal undertakings, it is most desirable that a high and uniform standard of account keeping should prevail throughout the country. The committee are doubtful whether it would be possible to prescribe a standard form for keeping accounts for all municipal or other local authorities, having regard to the varying conditions existing in different districts; but they recommend that the Local Government departments should invite the Institute of Chartered Accountents,the Incorporated Society of Accountants and Auditors, the Institute of Municipal Accountants in Edinburgh, and the Scottish Institute of Accountants in Glasgow to confer and report on the matters. The committee recommended that a uniform system of audit should be applied to all the major local authorities, the councils, counties, cities, towns, burgh, and urban districts.

div.head: BOLTON CORPORATION SCANDAL.
div.p: A BOLTON CORPORATION SCANDAL.
Action of the Town Council.

Keen interest centred in Wednesday morning's meet- ing of the Bolton Town Council because of the action of a sub-committee on what is known as the paving scandal,which action was known to have been approved by the General Purposes Committee—practically the whole Council—who had strengthened the reports by resolving "that the private works surveyor (a gentle- man who used to be deputy borough surveyor) and the two inspectors immediately under him be requested to tender their resignations of the respective positions now held by them under the Corporation." The sub- committee had been appointed on a statement of Coun- cillor Dr. Thornley, who had contended that in certain cases the Corporation and private owners were made to pay for work which had been improperly done, and for concrete which was not supplied to anything like the thickness specified. Other irregularities were hinted at. The committee had certain streets broken up to settle the matter. They reported "That the private works surveyor and the two inspectors have been very culpably lax in their direction and -supervision of the works which this committee has found to be very unsatisfactory." It was then discovered that there was a conflict between two departments, and the upshot is that the Private Works Department is to be abolished and the whole placed under the Borough Engineer. During the debate the Council strongly approved of DT. Thornley's stand, he being thanked by the Mayor, and it was decided that a special estimate of the loss should be made, with a view to the cost therebf being taken from private individuals to the right quarters. The resolution confirming the action of the sub-com- mittee and General Purposes Committee was unanim- ously carried. The disclosures have aroused Consider- able feeling.
CARNEGIE'S LATEST GIFT.-HALF-A-MILLION

TO HIS NATIVE TOWN. • Mr. Andrew Carnegie has intimated his intention of ,making a gift to his native town, Dumfermline, of half a million sterling in Steel Trust bonds. Some time ago Mr. Carnegie purchased the estate of Pittencrieff, near Dunfermline, and in now giving the half million he stipulates that it is to be employed in keeping up this- estate as a pleasure ground, and in the maintenance of. a theatre for the production of first class plays, for an exhibition of the arts and sciences, the encouragement of horticulture among the working classes, and the ad- vancement of .technical education in the district, which is the centre of the linen industry in Scotland. Con- siderable liberty is also allowed to the trust which is to be created for the purpose of administering the gift with regard to other methods of advancing the moral and material interests of the town.

A VIRAGO DT THE DOCK.

There was a struggle in the dock at the Borough Polioe Court on Saturday between a female tramp and Sergeant Cheney. The magistrates on the Bench were Mr. Birchall (who presided), Mr. R. T. Fairclough, and Mr. J.W. Hayward. The female tramp was a middle-aged woman nained Helen Keating, and she was charged with refusing to perform the task of work given to her at the Workhouse and also with assaulting John Constable, the porter.—John Constable stated that the prisoner was admitted into the vagrant ward on Thursday night, but she absolutely refused to do any work. She tried to get through the gates and used filthy language. She also got hold of one of the inmates of the house by her hair and pulled her to the ground. She waited behind the door for witness and struck him "right and left" with two large pieces of oakum. She had been twice previously convicted of drunkenness.—When the Chair- man announced that she would be committed to prison for three months she made a dash at Sergeant Cheney, who was in the dock, and struggled violently with him. A constable came to the sergeant's assistance and the prisoner was removed, but she shouted loudly for some time afterwards. MR. H. ROBERTS AND THE RAGGED SCHOOL.

Yesterday at the Warrington County Borough Police Court, before Mr. H. Roberts and other magistrates, Charlotte Barton, 12, Garden-row was summoned for assaulting Martha Green, 11, Garden-row, on August 3rd.—She pleaded not guilty.—Complainaatalleged that at eleven o'clock on Monday night she met the defen- dant In the street. Witness was carrying a bottle of beer and after some dispute defendant pushed her down causing her to cut her head with the bottle.—Defendant denied the offence and said complainant was drunk and fell Flown.—During the hearing of the case it transpired that complainant's child had been to Southport during the day with a number of children who were collecting on behalf of the Ragged School.—The magistrates dismissed the case.—The Chairman said he was only expressing his own opinion when he said it was a curious condition of things that a child should be used for the purpose of collecting money in a neighbouring town on behalf of the Ragged School when at the same time the mother of that child was able to find money to buy drink. It certainly afforded a great deal of food for reflection.

div.p: Warrington Borough Pollee Court. Minor Cases.

SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. Bizchall (presiding), R. T. Fairclough, and J. W. Hayward. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—WiIIiam Curley, who made his 31st appearance, was fined 10s. and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street on Friday night. MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks (presiding), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Thornton, and Messrs. Birchall and S. Wright. WEEK-END DRUNKENNESS.—The following were fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly :—Michael Preston, 1, Chapel-lane; Wilhiii Mulligan, Rose and Crown-street ; Joseph Webb, of no fixed residence ; and James Leigh, of iLiverpool.

TUESDAY.—Before Aldermen Sutton (in the chair), and Smethurst, Dr. Fox and Mr. J. R. Young. VIOLENT PRISONER AND HOSTILE CROWD.—William Jackson Lawless 1, Spencer's-yard, Tilley-street, was summoned for hexing been drunk and disorderly on School Brow on July 25th, assaulting P.C. Hughes, and damaging his uniform.—The Constable stated that he was called to the "Manx Arms" to eject the defendant who was drunk. He refused to leave the premises when requested by the landlord and with some difficulty witness got him outside. Defendant then made use of very threatening language and witness took him into custody. Lawless was very violent and in the struggle damaged witness's tunic to the extent of ss. They. fell to the ground and defendant then kicked him about the legs. A hostile crowd assembled and defendant was rescued and made off. Subsequently, witness visited the man's house in company ;with Sergeant Millais and P.C. ' Mriskett. On being accused of the offences alleged defendant replied "It's all right, but I did'nt tear the jacket." It was a boast in that neighbourhood that the police could not take a Crossley-street man."— Corroborative evidence having been men the Chief , Constable said he had received authentic inform- ation that there was a movement on foot in the neighbourhood in question to pay by ' subscription any fine which might be inflicted.—Alder- man Smethurst asked if none of the persons who helped to rescue the prisoner could be brought before the Court.—The Chief Constable pointed out that Hughes was a new officer and would not know the people in the crowd.—Defendant was fined 20s. and costs and ordered to pay the amount of the damage (£2 3s. in all) or in default a month': imprisonment.—Defendant said 4.8 would go to gaol. OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—MiChteI and Mary Clarke, re- 'siding at 2, Friars'-lane, were each fined ss. and costs, and Thomas Mannion, 2, Black's Yard, was fined 10s., for making use of obscene language. ACCIDENT AVERTED.—Rickard Culkeen Grappenhan was charged with having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and lurry in Knutsford-road at 4.45 the previous afternoon. The evidence showed that the vehicle nearly collided with il a tram car but an accident was averted by the application of the emergency brake—Fined ss. and costs.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Birchall (in the chair), and Aldermen Heaton and Smethurst.

ARREARS OP MAINTENANCE.—John Flannaghan, Hopwood-street, was summoned for arrears of mainten- ance due to his wife Ellen, amounting to £1 lls.—After hearing the evidence of both parties, the magistr ates fixed the amount of the arrears with costs at £1 2s. 6d., and ordered defendant to pay the money or go to gaol for 14 days. VAGRANCY.—AIfred Lee and Elizabeth Travis, of no fixed residence, were each sent to gaol for 14 days for sleeping in a house in the course of erection, in Orford- avenue, on Tuesday night.—P.C. Dyson proved the case THURSDAY:—Before Messrs. John Fairclough (in the chair) and Charles White. SLEEPING Our.—For being found sleeping in a 'bus in Messrs. Maginn's yard in Arpley-street, without any visible means of subsistence, Arthur Heywood.last from Liverpool, was, on the evidence of P.C. Maskett, sent to gaol for a month.

FRlDAY.—Before Mr. H. Roberts (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, Councillor Thornton and Mr. Hepherd. SCENE AT A THEATRE ENTRANCE.—George Johnson, last from Manchester,. was charged with having been m drank and disorderly Scotland road at 9.50 on Thurs- day night and with assaulting Joseph Willcocks at the entrance to the Theatre Royal.—P. C, Sankey stated that he was on duty in Horsemarket street and in consequence of information received he went,to the Theatre Royal. Prisoner who was drunk, was at the entrance making use of very bad language. Witness spoke to him and prisoner attempted to strike him in the face. He was then taken into custody and locked up—Joseph Willcocks, a checker at the Theatre, stated that he was on dnty at the entrance when prisoner, without the slightest pro- vocation, struck him in the face—Prisoner who was convicted of felony inJune,was sent to prison for 14 days.

ASSAULT IN A SHOP.—Thomas Stirrup, John Stirrup, and Kate Stirrup, 5, Admiral-street, were charged with assaulting Jane Ward, 46, Lord Nelson-street, on August lst.—Mr.Browne appeared for the complainant. —Some dispute arose between Thomas Stirrup and the complainant with reference to some clothing and it was alleged that Stirrup went to complainant's shop and made use of very bad language. He then struck her in the side with his clenohedlist, making her very sick,and afterwards kicked her on the ankle. The other defend- ants then came upon the scene and attacked complain- ant who had had to be medically attended in conse- quence of the assault.—Several witnesses corroborated this version.—Defendants denied the assault.—The magistrates decided that Thomas Stirrup had committed an assault but under provocation and fined him 6s. The other defendants were dismissed.

WIFE DESERTION.—Joseph Taylor, Hopwood-street, was summoned for deserting his wife Hannah Taylor,ll9 Manchester-road--Complainant alleged that owing to defendant's threats she was forced to leave her home, and defendant had since been living with her sister— Defendant said his wife went away of her own accord —A separation order was granted with 2s. 6d. per week alimony. PERSISTENT CRUELTY TO A WlFE.—Walter Ellis, 19, Phillip-street, was summoned for persistent cruelty to his wife Elizabeth Ann Ellis, 20 Erwood-street.—Com- plainant stated that defendant continually illused her when in drink and on Monday she was forced to leave him.—A separation order was granted defendant to pay 10s. per week towards the maintenance of his wife and children.

Mr. John Royle has declined to accept the Lord Mayoralty of Manchester for a geoond year. He told a deputation yesterday that there were other men in the Council capable of occupying the position and willing to take it, and he desired to see the honours properly dispersed.

div.head: AS WELL AS EVER.
div.p: AS WELL AS EVER.

From Ventnor, Isle of Wight, comes good news of a somewhat remarkable character. Mr. H. Drudge, of South Street in that town, had been for a long time a great sufferer from Backache of a peculiarly distressing kind. He describes it in this way : _

"I had pain;air-Oss-iiii-I;a:cii-:ln.d lions and if I had been sitting for any length of time I had great difficulty in getting up again and the pain would strike me like a knife going through my back." At last Mr. Drudge heard of a remedy called Dodd's Kidney Pills, which some of his friends claimed would curehim. He tried this medicine and was delighted to had that he was improving. He kept on with the Pills till at last he was completely cured and absolutely free from pain. He says:— am all right now. The pains have completely left me and I feel as well as ever I did in my life." Dodds Kidney Pills are very popular in Ventnor since the facts of Mr. Drudge's case became known.

div.head: Cricket.
div.p: Cricket.

That the Warrington eleven has been well served by its professional, Lynes, will be readily admitted by all who have followed the operations of the team dur- ing the season, and his " benefit " on Saturday was thoroughly earned. The large attendance was evi- dence of the general appreciation of the professional's work which has been of such value to the eleven in many matches. Manchester were the visitors to the Arpley enclosure and some interesting play was witnessed, despite the fact that the weather was not of the most .favourable description. The heavy rain at mid-day had a bad effect on the wicket and play was not commenced until a quarter past three. Although the result of the match was a draw the Warringtonians gave a very good account of themselves. Their innings had realized 145 for the loss of 9 wickets when the closure was applied, and four of the Manchester batsmen were dismissed for the aggregate of 24. At this stage more rain fell and the game was abandoned. .1

Lynes was in grand form and acquitted himself with great credit in both the batting and bowling depart- ments. He wielded the willow in spirited style and ran up the handsome contribution of 40, his best strokes including five fours and three threes. He bowled with capital judgment and captured four wickets for 9 runs.

The best batting exhibition was that of the home captain, J. W. Bibb_y, who placed 46 to his credit without a faulty stroke. He made no fewer than five fours. Other useful scorers were A. Thewlis (14), B. Silcock (11) and T. Houghton (10). No double figures were attained by any of the Manc,hester batsmen.

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

The Shield Competition in connection with the War- rington Anglers' Association announced in the Year Book to take place at Barrow Lock, Northwich, on September 12th, will take place in the Bridgewater Canal at London Bridge, on the same date.
The juvenile contest also announced to take place in the Bollin on September sth will be fished on that date in the Bridgewater Canal at London Bridge. Secre- taries of clubs and members please note.

Will the secretaries of local Angling Clubs please forward to the General Secretary of the Association, a list of the team or teams appointed from their clubs, to take part in the Worsley Canal Shield Competition and annual Championship on September sth, and from whom entry forms can be obtained on application?

Re the angling contest in aid of the District Nursing Association. An earnest appeal is made to the general public for assistance in support of the movement. An efficient committee will be appointed to receive dona- tions and will be provided with a book, endorsed and signed by the Chairman of the District Committee as authority for receiving and collecting contributions, without which authority no person is permitted to act on our behalf.

A large contingent of anglers took advantage of the holiday period, to iniulge in their sport, visits being made to numerous centres, including Rossett, Trafford, Northwich and the Bridgewater Canal. It is regrettable that Saturday and Sunday were so un- favourable from a climatic point of view, but it is hoped an enjoyable holiday was spent.

At Trafford, angling was somewhat slow, but an individual catch of dace is reported. The Weaver at Northwich also fished somewhat slow, and the same at Newbridge. Only Messrs. Cook, Owen, and others had fair catches, a perch of nearly 11b. being recorded. Fish in this river are not yet in feeding trim, probably owing to the heavy rains oflate, which invariably bring down much natural food.
The North Staffordshire canal at various points has fished fairly well.

The Bridgewater Canal continues to hold its own with many of the fisheries in our locality. J. Shepherd on the 2nd had a nice catch of fish from Preston Brook, while T. Worrall from near Moore was re- sponsible for a fair catch, baiting with paste. E. Hart and T. Buckley also had a good catch at Grappenhall; others also doing fairly well.

The somewhat boisterous weather of last week end somewhat hampered anglers in most waters, and it is hoped that a change will shortly ensue. It has come to the knowledge of the Worsley Canal Fishery Board that persons not holding the necessary permit fish the Bridgewater Canal, and this is to give notice that any person caught so fishing without such permit, will be prosecuted. The Board are determined to put a stop to poaching.

Entries for the Association contests at Beeston Castle, Thelwall and Agden will close on the 12th, 14th and 21st respectively. The draw for the two latter will take place near Thelwall Station and Agden Bridge.

The Howley Hotel Angling Society, to the number of 18, journeyed to Vale Royal last week end, to fish the first of their season's contests. Very fair sport was met with and the result, after the call of time was as follows :—I. Wakefield lib 13oz. 10 drms ; I. Sanson lib 3oz. 3drms ; T. Barry, lib 20z,:3drms ; J. Ward. 13oz. 27drms ; James Berry, 13oz. sdrms ; with F. Jolley, .J. Nicholson, G. Spencer and others following with lesser weights ; J. Sanson weighing a perch of 7ioz. for a special prize.

The Royal Oak drove to Vale Royal also to fish the contest; and here again a good return was made ; Messrs.- G; Ilamblett lib 131 oz ; W. Bate jun., lib 81oz. ; A. Shaw 11b 43;0z. ' Nunnerley llb ; with W. Hart, A. Mather and J. Whitfield following.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

A Bank-Holiday tour to Buxton had been arranged by the members of the Warrington Cycling Club, but owing to the unpromising weather on Saturday it was abandoned. Small sections of the club spent the week-end in North Wales and Mid-Cheshire, and had a fairly enjoyable time. The weather •on Tuesday evening was unfavourable and only five members turned out for the run to Crouton.

Eight members of the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Cycling Club turned out for a run to Southport last Monday. There was a strong head wind and the journey to the popular resort occupied four hours. A very enjoyable day was spent the various attractions being patronized.

Members of the Lovely-lane Cycling ,"Club are asked to nate a change in the fixture for to-day (Saturday). The place originally selected was Weston Point via Weaver, but on making. inquiries the secretaries found that the tides would be unfavourable for that run. It has therefore been decided to visit Northwich via Sandiway.
Fixtures. Warrington C.C. To-day (Saturday), - Delamere ; Tuesday, Newton-le-Willows.
Royal C.C. To-day, Delamere (Inter-club run with Warringto4 C.C.); Thursday, Great Budworth.
Lovely-lane C.C. To-clay, Northwich ; Wednesday, -High Legh.
Sankey Bridges Wesleyan C.C. To-day, Crana,ge ; Monday, Bucklow Hill.
Lighting up time to-night, $.55.

div.head: Rugby Football.
div.p: Rugby Football.

Warrington have signed on a new forward in George Thomas, of Newport, one of last season's reserve Welsh Internationials. He played in the trial games for Wales, and has a good reputation. The Club. expects .shortly to obtain the signature of a Northern Union County forward. In addition to transferring Burgess to Leigh, Warrington have handed over Landaff Smith, the one-time centre, to Wigan—for a consideration. They appear to mq to have done well out of the barter.

The well-known Cheshire and Lancashire forward, W. Oram; of Broughtoa Rangers, has seceded and thrown in his lot with Stockport County, who will endeavour to shape him into an Association full back. Oram was one of the finest forwards in the country, and the County manager believes that he can be made into a first-class back. He is on the heavy side, but is speedy, and has tremendous kicking powers.
