There is no holiday for THE UNIONIST FREE Parliament on the first FOOD LEAGUE. Monday in August.

The fact seems to have been so vividly present to Mr. CHAPLIN'S mind that he failed to remember that the bulk of the popula- tion would be holiday-making, and he was thus led into sending to the newspapers a long correspon- dence on the very day on which it would have least opportunity of getting read. He has, it seems, been approached by the Free Food League, a bo3y which is presided over by Sir Michael HICKS-BEACH on the subject of the distribution in his constitu- ency of literature bearing on the CHAMBERLAIN 1 policy. The League, it seems to us, is somewhat excessively polite. Before distributing its pamph- lets in a constituency represented by a Conserva- tive member it makes inquiry, as in Mr. CHAPLIN'S case, as to w'aether the member will object. Mr. CHAPLIN objects in a long argumentative letter, and it will thus come about that the electors in the Sleaford division will be deprived of so much enlightenment as they might receive from the publication of the Free Food League. We submit that the delicate consideration shown for the member is hardly fair to the constituency. The leaflets and pamplets issued by the Free Food' League are an important part of the evidence °Herod :in the "grand inquest of the nation.' Naturally a member who, like Mr. Chaplin, has determined to come down on MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S side of the fence will object to the circulation among his constituents of anything likely to make it appear that he has taken a course detrimental to national interests. Ho is thus able to pre- vent the distribuiion of the free food litera- ture where it is needed most, and to reduce the Food League to absolute ineffectiveness as regards himself. The officials of that body will, we imagine, find themselves forced into a more determined form of propagandism. It is easy to perceive why the present courteous method of proceeding has commended itself to them. They have been shocked, no doubt, by the methods of "Consistent, Birmingham." They have determined

not to imitate the tactics of Mr. VINCE. Mr. WINSTON CHURCHILL and others have complained that whilst the Government is alleged to be hold- ing an inquiry, and before any report has been made or any determination arrived at, their con- stituencies are being flooded by publications in support of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S views. The Com- plaint is a quite proper one, but no similar griev- ance could have been created by the general distribution of the Free Food League literature. The cases are not parallel. The Birmingham pamphlets are issued at the instance and with the authority of a member of the Government which purposes to be inquiring into the very matters which they have prejudiced Their purpose undoubtedly is, as Mr. WINSTON CHURCHILL affirmed, to undermine the position of members who are prevented from taking the field until the inquiry comes to an end. It is Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S position which makes all the difference in such a case. The Colonial Secretary ought to have felt bound by every honourable con- sideration to refrain from influencing the electorate in behalf of his views until the "grand inquest " was declared to have *come to a conclusion. If he had left the Government, as Sir Michael HICKS- BEACH has done, he would have been at liberty to do as he liked. Nobody could have complained of Mr. VINCE'S leaflets then except in so far as they are stuffed with misrepresenta- tions. But whilst he is in the Govern- ment and before his colleagues have definitely declared which side they intended to take in the " big fight," the distribution of the Birmingham literature partakes of the nature of hitting below the belt, a method of fighting to which so" accom- plished a bruiser" as Mr. CHAMBERLAIN should by no means betake himself. But no similar reasons can be urged against the operations of the Free Food League, which is as free to distribute its publications in any constituency as is, for instance, the Cobden Club. Its cautious politeness is a fine spectacle, no doubt, but it is not war. The num- ber of Conservative members who will object to the idistribution of anti-Chamberlain literature among their constituents is certain to be rather considerable, and the Free Food League seems likely to be left with a large amount of useless printing on its hands. The League voluntarily places itself in a position of great disadvantage in what will be a fierce contest. And with what result in Mr. CHAPLIN'S case? That whilst the circulation of the League literature is forbidden in the Sleaford Division, Mr. CHAPLIN rushes into print with a long piece of special pleading, and without waiting for any kind of reply.

The new POPE is a new THE NEW POPE. problem. If the accounts that are given of him are to be relied upon he is likely enough to bring to a close the long quarrel between:the Vatican and the Quirinal. But nothing can be said with any cer- tainty for the present. Cardinal SARTO, now to be known to the world as Pius X., was not even named among the possible Popes when the Cardi- nals were walled up in the Vatican. His election is another case of the triumph of "the dark horse." It is said that LEO XIII. had identified him as his successor, but this reams to be one of those stories that are invented for the occasion. At any rate,it only becomes known now that LEO is succeeded by Pope Pius X. There really seams to be something like providential guidance in the system ,by which Popes are elected. The men who are regarded as the popular candidates for St. Peter's chair seldom arrive at that lofty position. This might be because each of the electors is himself a possible Pope. Every Cardinal is likely to see the faults of his friend more clearly when that friend becomes a rival,and there is none of us who likes to put above himself somebody with whom he has been on cordial and intimate terms. Thus the election of a Pope, like the election of a Royal Academician, resolves itself into a process of elimination. The man against whom there are the fewest objections is likely to come oat at the head of the ballot in the long run; and just because the objections against him are few, and because he conquers by negative rather than positive merits, he may turn out to be the best possible choice. A raging and tear- ing Pope would be the worst possible head of the Papacy at the present :time. He iwould be cer- tain to break up the greatest religious organisation in Christendom. Closing the Cardinals up within doors which they cannot pass may possibly be as necessary a preliminary towards a just and dis- cerning choice of a Pope, as it was in those days when the election was liable to be disturbed by military violence or the more subtle compulsion of bribes. Shut out from the world, a man is driven back on himself and his own intimate thoughts. The great importance of.the act in which he is engaged is likely under, such circumstances to become insistent. He perceives, as he might not otherwise do, that he is called upon to discharge a duty to the world at large, not merely to please a few friends.

The little that we know of the new POPE proves that he has been chosen with honest intention. It is usually alleged that a POPE is chosen heeause he is an old man and because he is unlikely to live ong. Cardinal SARTO is 9f the same age as Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. He is of the age at which Cardinal PECCI became LEO XIII. It would have been possible to elect many older and much more enfeebled Cardinals to St. Peter's chair. That consideration may be pit out of the account therefore. The electoral poll has not had the fear of a fairly long life before it. A more important matter, and one which concerns the world no less than the Roman Church, is the fact that it has elected a Pope who is not only "no politician," but who has been civil and gracious to the Italian Throne. The problem presented by the election of Cardinal SARTO to the ',Pope- dom is, will he make friends with Italy? Will he abandon the absurd pretence that the PoPR is a prisoner within the Vatican? Will he recognise the fact that henceforth he can exercise no in- fluence over the Italian kingdom that is not founded in his spiritual authority? His past would suggest an affirmative reply to these questions.ll§But the real answer will be furnished by his demeanour after his election. Heirs apparent, as we know by many eKamples, always belie their early promise when they become Kings. This is sometimes the case with Popes. But Ptus X. is a likely man to make peace with Italy. Should he do so he will greatly strengthen his position. As for Italy, it has really nothing to gain by reconciliation, and it has something to lose. If the POPE" adopts" the Italian kingdom he will receive £300,000 a year, child that is a sum which overburdened Italy need not be too eager to pay.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield has departed this week for the Engadine, where he hopes to recuperate after his arduous labours in enunciating Free Trade arguments in reply to Mr. W. Peter Rylands. We are sure all our readers will heartily wish him boa voyage. As a parting shot Mr. Crosfield contri- butes another lengthy letter in answer to Mr. Rylands, which is, for some time at any rate, to be his last contribution on the subject. When ti he fight becomes keener and the election draws nigh, then we may expect a resumption of the warfare on the part of Mr. Crosfieid. He and Mr. Rylands are worthy opponents, and their discussion of this complicated fiscal question in our columns has, We are sure, bees of considerable help to our readers in forming their own decisions in regard to the policy of the country. Free Trade stands on a very firm basis, and we believe that, notwithstand- ing the clever arguments of his opponent, Mr. Crosfield has strengthened both foundation and superstructure.

Ratepayers who are anxious to know how the rates have been spent should apply to Mr. Fair- hurst, our painstakiag Borough Treasurer, for a copy of the abstract of the accounts of the Corpora- tion for the year ended March last. The abstract runs into nearly two hundred pages and forms a bulky ' tome. It is not the most interesting or entertaining volume that one could pick up but the recent awakening of interest in municipal affairs should cause the accounts of the Corporation to be more generally studied. That the accounts have already been carefully scrutinised is attested by the report of the auditors which appears on almost the first page cf the book. This is the first time we recollect seeing the auditors' report accompanying the accounts, but it is a departure which will be appreciated by all who are desirous of knowing what the auditors think of the accounts. On this head, the auditors report is reassuring, and bears the stereotyped. phraseology of everything being found " correct and "in order." Seeing that one of the auditors who signs the report was backed by the Non-Trading Committee, the report should be satisfactory to all. The aggregate balance sheet shows that the town's in- debtedness continues to grow and for the first time in the town's history it is over a million sterling, the exact figures at the end of March being £1,118,336 is. 10d. There are, of course, some valuable properties to show for this expenditure and the assets are estimated at £1,480,126 16s. 2d. thus showing a balance on the right side of £361,790 14s. 4d. These large figures will convey soma idea of the magnitude of the work of the Corporation, and as its importance continues to increase, it is essential that those who serve the ratepayers should do so with a single eye to the town's welfare.

The Committee on Munacipal Trading makes no secret of its conviction that the present system— or, to be quite correct, the lack af system—under which the expenditure of the various local governing bodies is controlled is unsatisfactory. The elective auditors of the great munici- palities are condemned (on the ground that "little interest is taken in the election" and "no complete or continuous audit is ever attempted by them"), and the district audi- tors of the Local Government Board, to whom County Councils, Urban District Councils, and London Borough Councils submit their accounts, are disapproved of;as not being usually accountants nor capable of adequate professional work. The recommendation of the committee is that the pre- sent form of audit including that by elective auditors, should be abolished, and that auditors who are professional accountants should be ap- pointed by all local authorities, subject to the approval of the Local Government Board, and not to be dismissed without the sanction of that Department. They would also increase very largely the powers of the auditor in dealing with accounts. They think that a vigilant and efficient system of inspection and audit will provide a safeguar for the ratepayers without the power of d surcharge and disallowance which at pre- sent exists in the Government audit. On thp face of things these recommendations look as if they might effect an improvement in the system o`,, auditing public accounts, but the great poill" which must not be lost sight of is that the report aims at the abolition of the elective auditor. This is a step in entirely the wrong direction, and one that will certainly be strenuously resisted. We yesterday interviewed Mr. Norbury Williams oh the audit question, and he was characteristicallY emphatic, as the report in another column shows, in his denunciation of so reactionary and danger- ous a proposal. The elective auditor is the people's sheet anchor,and they must take care that the power of appointing the men who shall super- vise the expenditure of their moneys is not sum- marily taken from them.

The twice adjourned meeting of the Town Council will be held on Tuesday, for the consider- ation, in the main, of the oft-debated municipal trading inquiry. Our readers will probably recollect that at the July meeting the resolutiun proposed by Alderman Balton indicating the lines on which an inquiry should be held was rejected on a motion by Councillor F. R. Roberts who desired time to give noticeof an amendment,and the Council meet- ing was adjourned to a special meeting fixei a week later. Subsequently this special meeting was abandoned and the business moved on to the agenda for the August meeting which was postponed last Tuesday owing to the holidays. We now arrive at the scene and time of action once more. Alderman Bolton has abandoned his resolution to its fate, but Councillor Tinnion has come to the rescue and again placed it on the agenda, which also contains the amend- ments proposed by Councillor F. R. Roberts The latter we commented upon at the time they were first made public, and we have nothing further to add, beyond emphasizing our opinion that we do not see the possibility of a.n inquiry being held at all on the lin as suggested by Councillor Roberts, for the simple reason that the Non-Traders will not agree to his conditions. The motion now in the name of Councillor Tinnion is the outcome of the deliberationb of a special joint ' committee of Corporation representatives and Non - Traders and will have to be accepted or rejected in. tote unless the Non Traders are prepared to make some concession to Councillor Roberts, and this, as we have already made clear,is highly improbable We do not, ourselves, consider the motion to be perfect, in fact we have a strong objection to the clause whereby "the Commissioners shall receiVa no remuneration," but if the special committee vs convinced of the practicability of the scheme then we are prepared to forego our objection in the hope of obtaining a settlement of this vexed and vexing question. Let us have an inquiry on any lines so long as it will be thorough and result in the public coming to a clear understanding as to the nature of the trading between members of the Council and the Corporation. At the present rate of progress there never will be an end to the agitation, unrest, and suspicion from which the town is suffering, and we hope sincerely that on. Tuesday evening the Council will take such a step as may tend to bring in sight the end of so un- pleasant a condition of public affairs.

"Question time" seems likely to become es recognised an institution in our local Parliament as it is in our national assembly. The Non-Traders are adepts at asking awkward questions, and Councillors Pemberton and Lord are once mere to the fore in this respect. Conn" cillor Pemberton has entered some queries in regard to the" Palace of Justice" and the con- tract with Mr. Davenport, while Councillor Lord still probes relentlessly the slack contract muddle; The discrepancy between his figures and those er the Chairman of the Water Committee is con- siderable, and it is in the interests of good geverf): ment that the matter should be made clear to all. The last-named Councillor also desires to knew' who authorized the attendance of the Town Clerk before the:Parliamentary Municipal Trading 0019" raittee, and whether the ratepayers are to beef the expense. These are all knotty quentiono eV" require official enlightenment.

The deliberations of the Museum Committee on 'Councillor Upson's branch library proposal have resulted in something tangible. It is recom- mended that four "delivery stations" be estab- lished on shop premises at an estimated annual outlay of 220 per station. The idea is to keep a small selection of books at each place and afford facilities to the borrower of obtaining through the branch station any book which may be in the central library. This appears to us to be an excel- lent beginning to an admirable scheme. We have no doubt that the extra facilities afforded will tend largely to extehd the habit of reading and mind- cultivation among the masses, to ,their obvious advantage. In time, doubtless, complete branch libraries will be necessitated, and even by then a considerable amount of public good will have been •done. It is also a wise purpose to take steps as intended to form " issue centres" in the elementary schools. The proposals generally are of great value, and indicate progress in a new direction, for, up to now, the Warrington Corporation has not , bothered itself very much withutilitarian szhemes. We are glad that something is at last being done directly for the education and uplifting of the ,people.

A resolution by the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee, "that the sett pavement in Horsemarket- -street and Orford-lane be repaired," will be hailed - with delight. We do not profess to be closely acquainted with Orford-lane, but we are sure that very few Boroughs in the country possess a main thoroughfare in so scandalous a state as is Rorsemarket-street at the present moment. it has for years possessed a surface not much superior to a river bed, over which traffic of all :kinds has jolted complainingly, and yet nothing has been done beyond a little excavating by first (me committee and then another, which has left the street worse than before. A well-paved Rorsemarket-street will be a god-send to the thousands of people who use the thoroughfare daily. It is to be hoped that the repairing will be thorough and not of that type which only accentuates the evil lumpiness of the untouched portions of the street.

To sit on a Coroner's jury is not a pleasant linty at any time. Even when a juryman receives :shilling as a solatium for loss of time he considers *himself ill-paid. The most unpleasant part of the work is undoubtedly the viewing of the dead body. At an inquest held at Stockton Heath on Tuesday, Mr. Whitley, the foreman of the jury, with charac- teristic outspokenness, asked whether it was imperative for the jury to view the body. The Deputy Coroner gave the only reply possible, i.e. that the viewing of bodies was made compulsory by law- One is almost inclined to agree with Mr. Bumble in" Oliver Twist" that" the law is a bass" in in- sisting upon the performance of such an un- pleasant and unnecessary duty by the jurymen. As was pointed out, the viewing of bodies does not add one iota of evidence as to how deceased met his death, and there is always the risk of the health of the jurymen being affected in the performance of this unsavoury task. Those who have had the experience of inspect- ing a body which has been recovered from the Water "after many days" will appreciate the objec- tions of jurymen. There have been two such experiences in the district this week, and 24 iurymen may be said to have endangered their health in carrying out a duty imposed by law. Reform is sadly needed in the law relating to Inquests and that part respecting the viewing of 'undies in particular.

There is a poignant satire in a question which is lajd by the Rev. E. F. Wills of the London Missionary Society to have been recently set in '3lle of the literary examinations in China. The Pig-tailed students, it appears, at Hupeh,sonae 200 lniles from Hankau, who desired the Chinese cinivalent of the B.A. degree, were asked the 'allowing conundrum: " When the teachings of the philosopher 11Elli that all should love one Itiother won the adherence of the people their 151diers refused to go to war. The State Churches :31 Western Europe are somewhat similar in their 'eaching, but when their armies and navies receive he order to go to war they all eagerly compete to ie first in the fioht, resulting in the slaughter of the enemy. What is the reason of this ? " It would be interesting to know what answers were given to this conundrum by the :budding iiteroiti of Elupeh. Probably the period when the teachings of the philosopher Meh were accepted throughout the Flowery Kingdom, and all the Chineseloved each other as brothers, is as mythi- cal as the Golden Age. Certainly the cultured Chinese have inconsistencies of their own to study, for in no land under the face of heaven is a clearer distinction made by the higher classes between *hat is just and what is expedient, between the truths which contemplation and the schools I)oltstfully profess, and the acts which custom and the law permit to those who are freemen of philo- *4o, phy. Still, it is an awkward question, and one vistinctly embarrassing to any Christian teachers there may happen to be in the neighbourhood.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
The Company's Warrington Obligations.
Statement by the Chajrman.

At the half yearly meeting of the Ship Canal Company Zi Thursdayat the new Midland Hotel, Manchester,the Chairman Mr. J. K. Bythell alluded to the recent liti- gation as follows: Thu suitbrought by the Corporation 41d the traders of Warrington was tried in January last A, fter:a hearing extending over nineteen days Mr. oastice Byrne gave judgment against the Company. Acting upon advice, and because of the very serious bature of the issues involved, the directors at once de. 'sided to appeal. The graver portion of the judgment, to The Company,consisted in the following declaration:"The kid depth of eight feet of water means eight feat of water below the lower water level, at spring tides, from time , to time; and does not mean eight feet below any Permanent datum line." Whilst he of necessity spoke 'Nth great reserve, he must tell the shareholders that 't Was impossible to foresee what the effect upon the revenues of the Company of such a declaration, if tnaintained, might be in future years. The directors mad no alternative but to take the matter to a higher Court. Meanwhile they were obeying the order by t'lliploying increased dredging plant. It was a matter for consideration whether any change could be made La the river which, whilst being advantageous to YVarrington, would mitigate the severity of the clause fl the 1885 Act, on which the judgment was based. He had along with Mr. Hunter, the chief engineer of the 'eanll, met the gentlemen concerned at Warrington, and all he could say at present was that the question was ,heing considered. The Company would have a bill in varliament next session, and i‘their Warrington friends willing to fall in with any reasonable suggestions, matter might be dealt with in that measure. More 'Luau that he was unable to say at present.

div.head: Traveller and his Employers.
div.p: A Traveller and his Employers.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, .fore his Honour, Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C. •10mas Warburton of Woolston, seed Messrs. R. ,11' bite & Sons, mineral water manufacturers, whose 'ocal premises are at Stockton Heath, for :£1 16s, Wages in lieu of a week's notice.—Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff and the defendant company *as represented by Mr. Fitzgerald, the local manager. ,'Plaintiff's case was that he was engaged by the t'efendants as a traveller and he alleged that the horses r,bich he had to drive were in very poor condition. 4leeently he had to go an 18 miles journey and •..??1 returning the horses were so exhausted that he had "u stable them at the Longford hotel. The following ,w4torning he was discharged without notice or an extra paelts wages—For the defence it was stated that intiff 'had not been discharged but was suspended tc)! a short time in order that the manager might in- View him. No wages had, however, been pai to ,Plaintiff, it was alleged, had been drinking—Mr. ;t?gerald also produced an agreement signed by the aintiff to work for 18s. per week. He was also to eceive commission. Plaintiff denied that he agreed this sum and defendant's representatives admitted tßat he was regularly paid 365. per week. They need fo t, however, pay any more than the amount specified the agreement.—His Honour characterised the fia reement as a trap and said it was not a credit to the 41. He gave judgment for the plaintiff for the 441101 int claimed.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
Coming Events

On S—aturday afternoon next the annual show in connection with Stockton Heath Garden Society will be held in the Church Room, Stockton Heath. Lady Greenall will perform the opening ceremony. A grand fancy dress parade and demonstration in aid of the funds of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution will be held at Warrington on Saturday, September sth. The Town Council.
The August meeting of the Town Council will be held on Tuesday evening at 6 o'clock. Some of the more important business will be found commented upon in our leaderette columns.

div.head: Pupil Teachers' Scholarships.
div.p: Pupil Teachers' Scholarships.

The Education Committee offer for competition not more than 35 scholarships of the valtie of and free tuition, tenable for one or two years at the secondary school, to boys and girls wishing to become pupil teachers, Particulars are published in our advertis- ing columns.

A Scalding Fatality. Yesterday afternoon, Mn.l S. Brighouse, County Coroner, conducted an inquest at the Police Station relative to the death of Thomas Hart, aged one year and ten months, son of William Hart, 3, Cyril Street.— Alice Hart, deceased's mother,stated that on Monday she was in the:act of removing a pan of boiling water, when deceased knocked against her. This caused the pan to tilt overand some of the water fell on deceased's face, neck, and chest. She took him to the Infirmary and he was afterwards attended by Dr. Leigh, but died on Tuesday.—A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned.

Voters Please Note! The new list of voters for 1903 is now published and affixed to the door of every place of worship in the Borough, and can also be seen at the Liberal Club, Bevvsey-street. Every Liberal who has been a house- holder for 12 months ending July 15th, last, should examine the list for himself, aad if his name is omitted, or if there is any error or misdescription of any kind whatsoever, he should inform Mr. Clayton, the Liberal agent, at once, so that the vote may not be lost. Lodgers who occupy one or more rooms of the clear value of £lO are also entitled to vote, and should claim immediately. Claim forms and all assistance will be readily furnished on application at the Regis- tration offices, Liberal Club, Warrington. All claims must be served upon the overseers on or before August 20th. The Show at Walton.

The fourteenth annual show in connection with the Warrington and District Agricultural Society will be held at Walton Park on Thursday next. The show yard opens at nine o'clock, and judging commences at ten. The whole of the morning will be devoted to the judging of shire and draught geldings, cattle, and pigs, hunter, hackney and pole pony Classes, while after luncheon the judging of the hunter classes will be continued,and the harness,jumpers and tradesmen's and tenant farmers' turnouts will also be judged, the show ground being closed at seven o'clock. There is a numerous entry in the various classes and visitors may confidently rely on seeing one of the best shows ever held in the district.

Death of Mrs. J. H. Cornell. It is with deep regret that we record the death of Mrs. Mary Gornall, widow of the late Dr. Gornall, for twenty-one years medical officer of health for War- ringtoxy who passed away at her residence, Ribbles- dale, Glrappenhall, on Wednesday. Ever since the death of her husband two years ago the deceased lady had suffered from an internal complaint, but she bore her painful and trying illness with great patience. She was in het sixty-second year. The late Mrs. G-ornall had lived in Warrington all her life. She was the third daughter of the late Mr. J.Guest,tanner,who was a prominent and respected townsman. In January, 1866, she was married to the late Dr. J. H. Gornall at the Warrington Parish Church. Dr. Gornall was at that time resident surgeon at the Warrington Dispensary and he was appointed Medical Officer of Health in 1880 The late Mrs Gornall was a Wesleyan, and during the greater part of her life attended Bold Street Chapel,. of which her father was for many years an active and much respected member. She leaves four sons and three daughters with whom the deepest sympathy is felt in their bereavement. The funeral takes place at the Warrington Cemetery to-day (Saturday). The cortege :will leave the house at p.m. and there ' will be a service at Bold Street Wesleyan Chapel at 1.45. 'An Interesting Catalogue.

One may obt-ain some idea of the enormous and varied output from the works of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. Ltd, at Dallain and Bewsey by consulting the admirably compiled catalogue which has just been issued by the firm. The first :part is de- voted to manufactured iron and steel,and the interesting information is imparted that the total value of finished iron and steel exceeds 2,000 tons per week, whilst the production of coal exceeds 800,000 tons annually. The second part of the catalogue will be of more interest to Warringonians as it deals mainly with the great engineering works which have gained the firm such a high reputation throughout the country. • There is a photograph of the elegant yet massive water tower recently erected by the firm at Trafford Park and other examples of the company's splendid work which find illustration in the books are the handsome bridge which carries the Wrexham and Ellesmere Railway over the Dee, a bridge of 225 feet span for the Liver- pool Overhead Electric Railway, the roof over the Riverside Station at Liverpool, a locomotive erecting shop containing over 4,000 tons of ironwork, and the fine Water Tank at Norton which forms such a con- spicuous landmark in the district. The catalogue certainly repays careful perusal. Bankruptcy of a Local _ Farmer.

At the Varrington Bankruptcy Court yesterday, before Mr. Registrar Ridgway, the public examina- tion of Daniel Percival, of School Farm, Appleton, was heard.—Mr. A. Browne represented the debtor and stated that the trustee (Mr. Mainwaring) was perfectly satisfied with the statement of affairs of the debtor' and therefore did not intend to cross-examine him. The liabilities were £982 6s. 7d. and the assets £422 18s. 2d, leaving a deficiency of £557 Bs. 3d. He attri- buted his insolvency to loss of cattle from disease, his own ill-health and heavy interest on loans. He commenced to farm about 23 years ago without capital. He estimated his loss Of cattle from disease at £450; loss by the death of a horse £2O; interest on loans £l5O. The unsecured liabilities included money borrowed and interest £519 7s. 3d.; seeds manure, cattle food &c., £203 16s, 4d.; smith's work £3B 15s. Gd. ; threshing, £9 2s. 3d.; beer, spirits, provisions &c., £26 19s. lid. ; clothing, boots, &c., £9 lie. 4d.; wages £2O, sundries £ll 2s. 6d. Mr. Johnson (assistant official receiver) asked for the examination to be closed.—The registrar closed the examinntion.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S TARIFF PROPOSALS.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S TARIFF PROPOSALS.
MR. A. H. CROSFIELD'S REPLY TO MR. W. PETER RYLANDS.
A Comprehensive Free Trade Argument.
MR. A. H. CROSFIELD writes :

Sir,—Before I proceed to answer Mr. Rylands' letter printed in your issue of July2sth, we may at least con- gratulate ourselves upon the fact that gr. Rylands has apparently revised his notion of how to estimate the value of a sovereign. It would have been a pity if his original statement that its yalue "depended "entirely upon the ease cw difficulty with which it is procured' had gone unchallenged. And it is a curious thing that when people beginto think in'sovereigns they are so apt to go wrong. We do not forget—how can we ?—Mr. Seddon's lamentation at hundreds of millions of golden sovereigns going each year to pay the foreigner for the "dumped " imports,w-hen all the time it is the foreigner who sends us more gold than we send him.. THE LIBERAL-PARTY AND FREE TRADE. j

Mr. Rylands is very surprised that the Liberal Party is solid for Free Trade since this makes the modification of our Fiscal Policy a "purely party question:, It has always been a feature," he says, "of progressive Liberalism to be prepared to entertain any policy, how- ever novel, if calculated to effect a desirableend,while to resent a departure from a policy of fifty years is a sign by which, above everything else, a Tory is known." . Of course it is true that a Liberal prepazed to con- sider anypolicy on its merits, but it is asad misunder- standing of Liberalism to imagine that its reforming zeal is never content to let well alone. No one dis- putes that in the commercial struggle every care ought to be taken to guard our national position, but Liberals (and for the matter of that not only Liberals but many Unionists. including three Unionist Chancellors of the Exchequer) believe that Free Trade is as essential to our prosperity as ever it was. When the keystone of the arch of our fiscal system is being tampered; with, it is playing with words to say that a Liberal ought to be eager to see if a "novel "experiment will succeed. As to Air. Rylands' statement that "manufacturers are strongly in favour of a change in our fiscal policy," we have to await the evidence f)r this much too sweeping assertion. No one doubts that soul& manufacturers would like a return to Protection, but it is not time to assert this of manufacturers as a class. In one industry not altogether unimportant in Lancashire—the cotton trade—masters and nten have jointly declared their con- viction that the welfare of their trade "can only be maintained by the policy of Free Trade!' ' THE UNITED STATES ANALOGY:

One or two other subsidiary points before I come to the; main proposition put forward by M. Rylands. I am not conscious of having set up arguments which no one has ever put forward, merely to be able to demolish them—that is another general statement which calls for no reply so long as the details are not forthcoming. Nor is it the fact that I "seriously misrepresented" Mr. Rylands' reference to the United States. lie com- pared the States to the British Erhpire and it was perfectly pertinent to point outs that no one • now imagines that we can secure the Fdee Trade within the British Etnpire which as a fact already obtains.: within the United States. No one disputes that the United States is a prosperous country, but not even Mt. Rylands asserts;that her prosperity now and in the future must depend upon • the maintenance of Protective Tariffs:

div.head: HIGHER WAGES.,
div.p: HIGHER WAGES.,

One other word before we discuss the main proposi- tion. Mr. Rylands is very prop *rly chary of seeking to prove that Protection would lead to a general advance in wages. He takes especial pains to point out that he" never assumed anything of the kind." A workman is to get the same for piecework and time work but he is to have a full week's work. PO work- men at present in full employment therefore, Preferen- tial Tariffs will, according to Mt. Rplands, increase the ;vst of living without increasing the rate of ' wages to meet that cost. Well, that i a very vital question and it will be interesting to learn what oar working men and working women in Warriagton, whom it most vitally concerns think about it. But it is well to remember that the Preferential Tariff proposals came not from Mt. Rylands but from Mr. Chamberlain and the Colonial Secretary so far from denying that the rate of wages will-be increased,definitely asserts it. Here dsan extract fr'om his letter to a working man dated June 3rd : "Even if the price of food is raised; the rate of wages will certainly be raised in greater propor- tion."

Those who will have to pay the increased wages have naturally taken fright at this promise. But it has been made, and Mr. Rylands cannot be allowed to run away from what is an integral portion of the scheme Mr. Chamberlain bids us accept at the peril of losing the Empire.

div.head: MAIN PROPOSITION.
div.p: THE MAIN PROPOSITION.

' I now come to what I have called Mr. Ryland' "Main Proposition. Here it is in his own word's:— " My contention isnot that the taxation of food stuffs would be in itself an advantage to the .coni- ' munity, but that the sacrifice involved would be far more than •counterbalanced ' by the additional ' employment which would be given- to the people through the increase of our export trade resulting from Preferential Tariffs placed upon British Manu- , factures entering our COlonies." Mr. Rylancla quite agrees that the taxation of food is " to the disadvantage of the community," but it is the price we ought to pay for preference in the Colonial Markets,.

div.head: VALUABLE ADMISSIONS.
div.p: VALUABLE ADMISSIONS.

There are valuable admissions in, this statemeat of the case. Elsewhere Mr. Chamberlain's supporters are trying to prove that as the result of 'taxing food no one —no one in this country—willlbe a penny the worse. The'," nanny Budget "will be left" undisturbed " says one of the f‘ authoritative "articles appearing in the " Birmingham. Post." Mr. Ryland, to his honour, will have none of this pretence.. He admits in the most explicit fashion that the taxation of food will involve " sacrifice ?' on the part of the 40,millions in the .IVlOther Country: he claims that the compensation is to come in the great access of trade we are to gain in the Colonies. POSSIBILITIES OF COLONIAL TRADE:

Mr. Rylands quarrels with some figures 1 gave as to the trade of the Colonies (figures, which I mayysay at once, were perfectly correct),,andsays "The Colonies at the present time, however nutch Mr. Crosfield may sneer •at,the volume of their-trade, import £250,000,000 sterling perannnm." (Parenthetically let me say that I never sneered "at the Colonies. Those who, do that are the .Protectionists who rate their loyalty to the Empire so low as to argue that it depends upQn the ma- tenal'advantages they are to.,get from the, new fiscal policy). Mr. Rylands.adds "Great Britain supplies the colonies with about £100,000,000 of their requirements out ora total of about £250,000,000. If we could secure- £50,000,000 out of the remaining., £150,000,000 the. benefit de- rired by this country would be im- mense. . ." .kndiagain "We have it as a‘frect that the Colonies import £150,000,000 sterling of goods each year from coun- tries other than Great Britain. There is thereforea 1 large and growing, trade for the Bri tikh -Manufacturer to exploit."

div.head: REAL-FIGURE
div.p: THE REAL-FIGURE

This is such a glorious and glowing, picture that it really seems a pity to, spoil it. But it; has to be done,. In the first place in order to get the. 2,250,000,000 3rr. Rylands has taken, not the imports of the Colonies. (i.e., the self-governing Colonies) but all the rest of the Empire including India! As a fact,,the imports of the Colonies according to the last available return anwunt to £124,000,000: Of this total £50;000,000 comes from foreign countries.E)mmination of-the £50,000,000 shows that more than, hall consists of raw material and goods that we could not supply, and that a liberal estimate of the'goods that we could supply now-obtained from foreign countries, is- £20;500,000. But this is by no means all. This £2o,soo)ooo,includes £10i000;000 for Canada where the British Manufacturer has- already the adNantage of 33N per cent preference. We must therefore rule out Canada, redUcing the total a trade we might capture if the foreigner were shut out altogether tc. £10,500,000 • PREFERENTIAL TARIFFS IN PRACTICE. .

But the notion that even with prefexenceour Colonies I will at once care or be abba to buy all they want from the Mother (Country is a childish illusion and can actually be demonstrated to be so by a study of the effect of the Canadian Preference. British imports into Canada have increased in amount, but that is because of Canadian prosperity. Relatively the British share in 1902 Of Canadian Trade is precisely what it WitS in 1898. T take the years given by Mr. Ryiands. Here is an iikaminating table tiakon from Canadian Oflioial returns: Imports into Canada. Percentages. From the From the From other trted K'gdom.United States. Countries.

The explanation of this carious result is in the Canadian tariff,which, while it admits most raw materials free, is almost prohibitive against the products which the United Kingdom largely exports. Moreover in one case—that of cotton goods—the duty was raised before any preference was given. rhe United States, which sends large quantities of raw materials to Canada, Oays on an average a much smaller percentage.on its goods, although nominally it obtains no preference. Between the years 1897 and 1902 the average, &toy on British goods fell from 2PI per cent to 17'1 per cent; American goods from 14•3 per cent to 132 per cent.— Great Britain with a preferentlat tariff paid, that is to say, four per cent more duty than, the United States. As to the poor results of the preference accorded by Canada we have further evidence from Mr. Chamberlain himself. Speaking to the Colonial Premiers at the Colonial Conference in. 4nly,, 19,0 A itsed. mmrds . .

"I have-to say to you that what* cannot but 'grate- fully acknowledge the intention .of this pi toposal. and its sentimental value as proof of goodwila and affec- tion; yet its substantial results Nsys been • altogetftsr disappointing to us, and I think they.' must have been equally disappointing to its promoters."

div.head: BENEFITS OF SCIENCE.
div.p: THE BENEFITS OF SCIENCE.

It is seldom that any discovery of science is such as will benefit all classes of people. Some of the greatest discoveries of the age, while they have proved directly oeneficial to thousands, have also, at least for a time,- injured other thousands. Even some of the best medi- cinal preparations, however much they may do to remove one class of disease, or suit some constitutions, at the same time either deepen the hold of another disease, or leave it entirely untouched, or if they benefit one class of patients, they. may injure another. :Now the great need of the age is some scientifically arranged preparation which will cope effectually with the prevalent diseases of this country, which will be certain to do good when fairly tried, which will be equally adapted to the needs of the mer- chant and the workman, the professional man, and he who wins his bread by the sweat of his brow, the student, the clerk, the factory hand, the miner, and the roadside labourer. It should be, too, such a preparation a contains no injurious ingredients, and which may be taken with impunity by the weakly child, or the delicate lady, as well as by the stronger constituted man. Such a discovery would deserve to be called The Perfection of Medicinal Preparations, and would indeed be an Invaluable Boon to Suffering Humanity. Now this much needed boon has been found, has been tried, has been proved, and wherever proved, it has been found satisfactory. We refer to Gwilym Evans' Quinine Bitters, the Vegetable Tonic, which when once tried, has been always recommended, and has proved successful when all other medicine has failed to give rerief, and we may say further, that it has proved permaaently beneficial, when other pre- parations at best only gave temporary relief. div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S TARIFF PROPOSALS.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S TARIFF PROPOSALS.
[Continued from page 51
ONE-SIDED FREE-TRADE V. PROTECTION.
Something about the Cobden Club.
MR. H. P. HUGHES writes:—
I'4l,
if

Mr. Harold Cox, secretary of the Cobden Club, is writing—l presume officially—to the Wasrington press, thus, as it were, putting the club officially forward as a responsible Free-Trade champion. Now with Mr. Cox, personally, the remarks I am about to make, have noth- ing whatever to do. He may be, and probably is, the most estimable of men. Unless personally hit, I always try to avoid unnecessarily wounding individuals. This is a free co-mtry, and, in his capacity as a private citizen Mr. Cox's opinions would be entitled to reoeive every couttesy ; but the consideration due to a private gentle- man is one thing, and the criticism of a public institu- tion is quite another. My present observations are strictly impersonal, and apply only to the system or institution that calls itself the Cobden Club. My theory is. that, any institution or system is open to public en- quiry, and public criticism or attack, just exactly is proportion as that institution or system steps officially and aggressively—outside of its ordinary business or private. routine capacity, into the turbulent arena of public affairs. Very well, the Cobden Club, officially and publicly through its worthy andable secretary, has offered public instxuction, warning, and advice, upon the great fisca question of the hour ; so to return the complimenti public opinion is surely entitled to ask who and/ what is the Cobden Club? It is only a few months, since this very question was under discussion in the London press, but possibly, the Cobden Club authorities do not give us "provincials," in Warrington, credit for being so far advanced as to know what goes on in the London papers, or we perhaps might not have been favoured with Mr. Cox's r6cent authoritative and official letter. To put the case into a practical form, will Mr. Harold Cox,as secretary, kindly inform the Warrington public, through the local press, what is the total membership of this mighty Cobden
'Club, and then tell us the proportion of foreign names in that list of members?

Mr. Harold Cox, officially, as secretary, need not hesitate, on the alleged score of business-privacy, to give the exact information, as an unchallenged approximation of the figures was published—only a short while ago—by that King of the British Imperial Press, the "Daily Mail." It is curious (to say the least of it) to see the Cobden Club daring—again and so soon —to pose as a public authority andadviser upon British fiscal policies. A paper, with a daily average circula- tion of over a million copies, becomes a vastly power- ful and speedy engine for moulding public opinion. The authorities of the Cobden Club may rest assured that some of those million copies reached every nook and corner of the island, with the result that the status, influence, or prestige of the Club—as a disinterested standard of authority upon fiscal questions—perished— for ever—from the moment that the British public dis- covered that a large proportion of the membership consisted of foreigners. At the time of the recent newspaper revelation or exposure, I should imagine that the general public impression would be, that the Cobden Club was a sort of political wolf in sheep's clothing. In other words, the general feeling was, that a lot of foreigners, whose respective native countries be.nefit largely (too largely) by Britain's one- sided free-trade policy, obtain membership of a vener- ated national institution (as we mai almost term it), like the Cobden Club, and, from that apparently most disinterested and orthodox watch tower, these foreigners (through their official secretary) shout lustily—an', no doubt very heartily to poor simple John Bull :—"Stick fast to Free-trade, John, for the Cobden Club is with you!"

Just to relieve a soMewhat dry subject, let me pleas- antly observe that our great national humourist and satirist, Mr. W. S. Gilbert (of Gilbert and Sullivan fame), would surely delight in embodying, in some new

comic opera, a so-called British institution which actually paid about half of its expenses—including about half of its Secretary's salary— from the subscrip- tions of members whose trade interests, or family ties, or both,were almost entirely bound up with Continental protectionist countries. I respectfully offer the "notion" to our British Juvenal,Mr. W. S. Gilbert for. if the recent "Daily Mail" version is correct (and I never saw it contradicted), this curious and paradoxical Comic-opera libretto is as true as it is hugely grotesque or burlesque. Before posing any more, as a sort of national and quite infallible authority on fiscal policies, the Cobden Club surely owes it to itself, and to the British public, to furnish British credentials and to establish British bona-fides. The English,Trish, Scotch. Welsh and Colonial members of the empire can com- fortably settle this great Protection or Free-Trade question, without any help from the cosmopolitan gentry wh. are said to constitute more than half of the existing na3mbership of the Cobden Club. Mr. Cox will find full particulars, upon which I have based these observations, in the "Daily Mail" of 29th November 4rd December last year. Leaving the Cobden Club incident, and passing along to the general subject.—l would mention

that, when an approximate analysis of the Protection v Free-Trade votes, in the present House of Commons was given, the other day, in a leading London paper;many people were greatly surprised to see that the votes are reckoned as being almost equal. It is a sign of the times, surely ! I well remember when I was so isolated in my opinions, that I'vras regarded as a mild sort of lunatic, by my iends, for advocating protectionist doctrines, which,
A

for many years were °illy held—or at any rate, openly expressed—by a few, here and there. Slowly,but surely a revolution of national opinion is proceeding, and we see how history repeats itself :—ln 1750, Britain was Protectionist, apparently beyond hope of change: in 1850, Free-trading—also apparently beyond possibility of alteration; but who can tell what 1950, or even 1910, will have to say upon this question? Each generation should thoroughly overhaul its own fiscal policy, and decide what system is most favourable to the then ex- isting set of conditions. In France, the fiscal policy is adjusted every ten years : but, in Britain, we are tied to a fetish, or to a method of hero-worship. A dead man's hand binds us tightly to a system long after that dead man, if now living, would have ventured to maintain that his theories were still as active and virile as when he originated them.

Lord Beaconsfield's epigram, upon our national nfatuation, clearly shews what he thought of our one- sided free-trade policy. His view was summed up in eight words, namely, that Britain had "Locked the door, and thrown the keys away." I take his meaning to be that we had, with almost ostentatious emphasis, told the nations of the earth that they might treat us just how they liked in trading matters, and, under, no possible combination of circumstances whatever, would we retaliate. The nations have—with their tongues in their cheek—taken us at our word, for many years, but, at last, the British worm of public opinion is turning , and is beginning to hunt for that "lost key" to open I what I would term the two-sided door that is marked I "Treat others as they treat you." As years have swept by, the British people have rather lost faith in their one-sided free-trade door, marked "Treat other i as you I would like to be treated." Our free-traders of to-day are living upon the theories and plPtitudes of fifty or sixty years ago, and they offer us smart and telling I• phrases, in place of practical facts. For instance, I should be glad to receive, from any free-trade friend, a list of, say, twenty Home-trade or Home-Market industries that are prospering as a result of Free-Trade. My mind is quite open to conviction, but I must have solid facts and figures in place of smart phrases. Up to now, my experience has been that the old-time plati- tudes and smart phrases are more plentiful on the side of free-traders, and the hard facts of business experi- ences are inclining more and more on the side of the

div.head: protectionists.
div.p: protectionists.

An excellent illustration of the difference between free-trade theoryand practice occurred a few days ago: —Mr. Whiteley, M.P., has been busy himself, trying to demolish protectionist facts and figures, so, When try- ing to be little the imports of iron, &c., from Germany and America, he said that he" purposely omitted nails, screws, rivets, and scrap iron, because they are not large amounts." This sounded all right—and perfectly innocent and unsophisticated—until one of the leading nail firms in the country, Messrs. Grimshaw and Cape- well, of Leeds, took up the running, and gave him a bard rap on his statistical knuckles, as under We take exception to his (Mr. Whiteley's) statements, if the figures he gives are correct, and will leave you to judge whether the omission of nails, screws, and rivets is so trifling as to be omitted from his statistics. In his table of imports of iron, steel, &c., from the United States,he gives £735,000 value. From Germany he says we import £613,000 worth of iron and steel, &c." "Can it be credited that, of the alleged insignifi- cant items he omitted (viz nails, screws,and rivets), we have imported up to the end of June 1903, for six months, nails, screws, and rivets to the value of £274,082 ? this, doubled into a twelve months' im- portation, comes to £548,164, which is equivalent to a trifle under the total imports from Germany or the United States of all the iron and steel, &c. coming (according to Mr. Whiteley) into this country. So that, to be just, Mr. Whiteley ought to double his statistics of imports." "We may say that the bulk of nails, screws, and rivets imported into this country, to compete with our own manufacturers, are bounty-fed goods, and these come almost entirely from Germany and Belgium."

"These facts speak for themselves, the total weight per annum of these articles re.anhing the vast number of 48,000 tons, the bounty being the only obstacle to oar making them ourselves. "Summarising the position, we say From Germany. From America. Iron and Steel Nails, screws, and rivets (too insignificant for Mr. Whiteley, M.P., to mention), January to June 30th, 1903, £274,052; doubled for twelve months £548,164."

Many of our modern injudicious Free-trade champions, do more harm than good to their cause, by eagerly over- stepping their proofs; or by purposely or accidentally omitting material figures or facts. The public never, afterwards, take a man's figures or facts seriously—as they do not knowlwhether he is to weak too grasp the true bearing of national problems and statistics; or too disingenuous and eager to win his" points" to take the trouble to be accurate. Carelessness in the handling of statistics is regarded as even a, worse public offence than hanky-panky,—for most men would prefer, of the two, in business matters, to deal with • a rogue than a fool.

In my own mind, I use two types of analogy, to ex- plain to myself (for a man must teach himself, before he can hope to teach others) the operation of Free- trade upon our national welfare. First, I take the type, of a white ant, which, in some countries, will eat the very vital sap,and inside, of certain trees, while leaving the outside, apparently, as strong as ever. A country, like Britain, that—for many years past—has beensteadily increasing its imports of manufactured or partly manu- factured articles, is likely—in course of time—to share the fate of the tree that is infested by white ants, and to perish, like Carthage and Venice. Again, I take the sea-shore, when the tide is beginning to come in :—The people, walking on the sands, close to the water, are the first to realise the inflow; whereas people, a little distance further ashore, may safely wait perhaps an hour or two. The moral of my parable is, that the people close to the water are the traders first touched by unrestricted imports; and the people further ashore are those traders that do not as yet— directly—feel the power of the rising ride of imported manufactures. The parable may be further developed, by making an analogy for the eddies, that, sometimes, surround and cut-off the people who think themselves far enough inshore to be quite safe. In the last two or three years, we have seen several departments of trade quietly—and yet as it were suddenly—surrounded and engulfed, as, for instance, our Morganised Merchant Shipping. This set of metaphors brings me to some practical illustrations of the people nearer to, or further from,

the rising tide of imported manufactures. Take cotton and soap as examples of the people who, apparently, are I at present safe from the inrush of the flowing tide. Mr. W. H. Laver, of Port-Sunlight fame, is probably one of the greatest living business-administrators. No one respects or appreciates his organising genius more than I do. He recently took occasion to preach Free-trade, and he can easily do this, because he had a business whioh, so far, is not touched, seriously, by foreign competition. If his commodity was, for instance, as open to foreign attack, by a bounty-fed system, as nails, screws, or rivets, he would—probably at this moment— be trembling for the safety of the four millions or thereabouts, invested by his shareholders. Mr. A. H. , Crosfield; being an honoured member of a local firm, I , need not saymore than to ask your readers to apply the , Port Sunlight 'anology; and—taking the protectionist point of view—see how Mr. W. P. Rylands, and Mr. E. W. Bindloss, typify the people closer to the rising , tide.

When a man is preaching Free-trade,asic him what he- earns his living by, and then you will—almost invari ably—find that, if he is a rabid free-trader,he has either ' never seriously studied the subject, or he is, as yet, safely out of reach of early danger from the tide of imported manufactures. The few exceptions to these' two rules, you will generally find to be "faddists.' who are at angles with everybody and everything. Self- preservation is the first law of nature, and it is quite as true in nations as in individuals. To bring about the present extraordinary condition of things, in which the

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 8, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 8, 1903.

country and the House of Commons has almost reached a point of equal voting upon Free-trade and Protection, we may depend upon it that a good many departments of business must have keenly suffered from the rising tide of unrestricted imports of manufactured or partly manufactured goads. Once it passes the half-way, we shall soon be in a position to erect a jetty, or break- water, in the shape of judicious taxation which, in its turn, will become a relief upon the present heavy burden of Imperial taxation, and in addition, will ensure more security of employment to the twelve millions of Britishers, who, at present, are estimated to be only living (cora week to week, in an impoverished, semi- pauperised sort of existence.

With a few figures representing Capital, output or pro- duction, and average yearly competition from imports in soap or leather (and the same theory would apply to any industry that is still shouting "Free-trade") dur- hag, say, the last ten years, I could—approximately— guess how long it would take Mr. Lever, Mr. Crosfield and Mr. C. E. Parker to desert Free-trade and become strong protectionists. It is safe to assert this, because the present growth of public feeling, in favour of Protection; has been, itself, simply recruited from business people who, after being brought up in orthodox free-trade doctrines, have been reluctantly forced, by circumstances, to reconsider the position. It is gentlemen of a very high order of intellect, such as the three names I have given, who become the most powerful advocates of Protection, when once converted. A convert is always enthusiastio and his zeal is in proportion to his ability, so we may expect much from the conversion, to Protection, of such capable business gentlemen. A witty Statesman or publicist said, not long ago, that, on this free-trade question—we Britishershad " not enough sense to come in out of the wet." If he will wait—at most—from five to seven years—he will find that our Protectionist umbrella is up. John Bull is said to be a dropsy, slow fiat-footed type of individual; and I think it was Mr. Gladstone who said that he soon went to sleep again, even after being wakened up, but there is every sign of him—thoroughly and effectively—arousing himself, when he once fully realizes that his Free-trade pocket is being quietly picked of the wages of his workpeople and of the capital of his middle and upper classes. jln Messrs Grimslaaw and Capewell's above quoted I letter, mention is made of bounty-fed goods. I wonder if our trade union leaders ever giveserious consideration j to]what "bounty-fed " means? Continental nations, in order to encourage their home industries, pay a bounty or bonus upon exported goods of certain types, with the tragic result (from a British Capitalist and Workman's point of view) that such goods come to this country below the cost at which they could possibly be made here, and then to be sold at a reasonable profit. It is bad enough for Freertraders to have to face the com- petition of foreign fair labour, but to face la bounty-fed competition with Free-trade is hopeless. j Of course:some of my extra-smart Free-trade friends say that this bounty-fed system is grand, and thac it would be still better if we could get the goods for nothing and walk about with our hands in our pockets; Ibut these simple but well-meaning friends quite over- look the great big fact that this bounty system not only ruins the British Capitalist, but it also destroys the wages fund, upon which we all live. Even at best, I Iwould maintain that heavy imports of manufactured or I partly manufactured goods, cause what political econo- mists term an endless displacement of Capital and labour—people hurrying from decaying home industries, and over-crowding or congesting, with labour and capital, the few that remain in fairly good condition. As so many business people, in Warrington, knew the late Mr. E. W. T. Richmond, I am sure that a free-trade anecdote, relating to that great and kindly business man, will be appreciated ;—Some (ight Or nine years ago, I had the honour of being an evening's guest at his residence in Winmarleigh-street, and the topic of Free- trade (then a very rare topic indeed) somehow came up. Mr. Richmond was not only an uncommonly well-read man, but he was also a capital debater, and he ran all over me, as it were. Of course, I soon found that my only chance lay in bringing the generalities "home," so j I said—" Mr. Richmond, supposing that there were in this country, say, ten thousand of American, German, or Belgian Gas Cooking-Stoves, and with larger and larger supplies being manufactured abroad, and only waiting for shipment to English ports, where would you be? Your works, and Fletcher Russell's, and the other Gas Stove Firms would very soon be closed." He looked at me, and, and,—changed the subject! I had touched him upon the most human of all spots— self-preservation. Free-trade was all right, so long as it kept off gas stoves; and so it is with all of us. The "Manchester Guardian," Mr. Whiteley, M.P., and the cotton operatives, and the soap people—all thoroughly honest and well-intentioned—are not troubling, so long jas their house is not on fire. If they had to face a j "bounty-fed" competition, it might make all the differ- ence in their point of view. Mr. Richmond—though only at that time about 29 or 30 years old—was in personal touch with over sixteen hundred towns and j cities; andhe travelled something like 20,000 miles a year, so he understood many distinct sets of trading iconditions, and was therefore, wilh his brilliant intellect prepared—instantly as it were—to translate gib War- ringtonword "Gas-stoves" into carpets in one town; boots in another; woollen goods in another, and so on, j and so on, and soon. I had touched the right chord, to bring the bearings home to him, and I did not need to say a word more. He did not tell me he was convinced but I was sure that I ha' 1 left a favourable impression; , or what we would now call a condition of "open mind.', I have made many converts to protectionist ideas, by bringing in some local or personal interest. Thus, a whileago, an egg merchant, from Shudehill Market, visited me, and I explained to him the nefarious system of taking French eggs to Belfast; re-crating them, and selling the eggs as "Irish." Ask in any grocers shop for a "French" egg, it is doubtful if you get one—and yet they come to this country in millions. If Ireland had agitated for Protection, in place of Home Rule, these many years past, she might have been, to-day, a most prosperous country. This is my fifth letter, and the subject is so many- sided that I could easily go on to the twenty-fifth, but your readers may be getting tired of me; and then there are other writers probably waiting for space, so I will try to condense my story into two more letters— making seven in all. In my rough notes, I have many headings still untouched-'-in fact, I wrote 42 separate Protectionist headings; from memory, in my first rough draft but other writers will probably cover those I omit. In the two final letters, I hope to give some interest- ing quotations from Mr. Carnegie; and will also try to show some of the cotton-trade bearings upon Protec- tion.

P.S. In to-day's (Monday's) "Times," there is a re- markable letter, written by one who, for thirty Tears, has been "watching with alarm the development of foreign industries, and their invasion of our domains. He describes how factories have sprimg up on Rhine- land, and converted a pastoral into a manufacturing country ; how Bohemia . has opened hundreds of sugar factories, as our refineries closed: how Austria has captured our glass trade; and how even Poland has, be- come an active competitor of England. In every home, in every shop, in every factory of this country, are foreign goods freely imported into England, in compe- tition with our own productions, while British goods can only enter Continential countries through the needle eye of a restrictive tariff." If I could say so, without being thought irreverent, I would add the moral, "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear."
French import duty on 1878-1882 1898-1902 wheat per quarter. f is. od. 12s. 2d. Average price of wheat 1 per quarter in France. j 495. 10d. 375.3 d.

"We fancy" (says "The People ") "these most signi- ficant figures will surprise a good many people who believe the Radical tale that a tax on food-stuffs must necessarily mean:a corresponding rise in the price of them to the consumer in that country." I wonder if Mr. H. P. Hughes thinks that the above quotation and remarks will "gull" the average Radical. A more glaring case of what would be termed the inducti falsi could hardly be imagined. Increased pro- duction, bountiful harvests, and cheapened transit have lowered the natural market price of wheat, in France,as elsewhere, by 245. 3d. per quarter, an advantage (to the consumer in that country) which has, however, by means of the increased tariff, been whittled down to 12s. 7d. in other words, the increased tariff of us. lid. has resulted in an increase of us. Bd. upon the natural market price of the wheat. Now the case in England is something like this:— Average price of wheat 1878-1882 1898-1902 per qr. in England 4Bs. 9d. 245. 6s.

The result here is that the consumer in this country gets the whole advantage instead of about half. If the 12s. 7d. saved is an advantage to the French people, surely a saving of 245. 3d. is to us in England still greater benefit.

_ The tworkman's letter dodge is an old trick of" The 'People." I fancy it all came out of "Fleet-street." That letter is just too handy and too opportune to have the smack of reality about it. It will, when carefully sifted, come out as I have shewn the duty on wheat. Again we hear that the "dumping" of German iron goods isruining the iron trade of England. The figures for the past year show. England's iron!trade £140,000,000 The "dump" (from Germany) £589,000

For this small "dump "of about half a millionagainst I .C 140,000,000 is the entire fiscal system of the country to be changed? Figures during the past five years showed that profits in the iron trade had risen 300 per cent. Again our exports of all sorts of British. goods to our Colonies last year amount to £60,364,000. Our exports of manufactured goods only, to Germany £17.009.000, France £10,500,000. Russia £6,500,003, Belgium £7,400,000, United States £20,800,000, total £62,200,000 that is to say wesent more manufactured articles to five foreign nations, than to all our white colonies. Our exports to the same five nations are not decreasing but increasing. British exports to America, France, Ger- many, Russia and Belgium. In 1902 „ 1898 Increase 10,265,000

div.head: CHANGED AIR-INDIGESTION REMAINED.
div.p: CHANGED AIR-INDIGESTION REMAINED.
But Bile Beans Cured Her.

Many people fondly believe, that if they can only get a change of air, they will cease to suffer from indiges- tion, liver complaint, biliousness, or some similar ail- ment which may be troubling them. In this way, vast sums of money are wasted every year in stays at the seaside or in the country. "I often went away for a change of air," says Mrs. Brown, of Park View, Leven, "but derived very little good from it, and in a few days I would have indigestion just as bad I again. After any food I had most violent I pains, aocompanied with headache, sickness,and feelings of weakness. In the end I grew so debilitated, that I I could not do my housework. Sometimes felt quite hungry, but I actually dare not eat because of the pain it occasioned me "afterwaids. div.head: ANTI-VACCINATOR'S APPLICATION.
div.p: ANTI-VACCINATOR'S APPLICATION.
County Magistrates Refuse to Grant an Exemption Order.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, before Messrs. John White (presiding), T. Halton, and F. A. Frost, Thomas Heywood, Station-road, Penketh, applied for an order exempting,his child from vaccination. He said he had a conscientious objection to vaccination. At present the child was healthy and well and he wanted it to continue so. He did not think vaccination would do the child any good. The Clerk (Mr. H. Greenall) said that was not a con- scientious objection and asked the applicant to state the grounds of his objection. Applicant: I think vaccination is useless. The Clerk: Why do you think so? Applicant: Because it neither prevents nor mitigates the disease it is supposed to stamp out. The Clerk said that tp make a broad statement like that was not a conscieffious objection. Further questioned the applicant stated that he had had two of his children vaccinated. One of them suffered from a bad leg and he attributed it to vaccination. The Clerk: Has the doctor certified that it is due to vaccination. Applicant: It is not his policy to tell me that. - The Clerk: Oh, nonsense! The magistrates have no power to refuse your application if you satisfy them that you have a conscientious objection. Again questioned, the applicant said he had never asked his medical man whether the child's bad leg was due to vaccination. The magistrates I declined to grant the application until the applicant could give better reasons,

div.head: GULF STREAM AND OUR CLIMATE.
div.p: THE GULF STREAM AND OUR CLIMATE.

The statement, often repeated by meteorologists, that the warm water of the Gulf Stream is not carriednear the British Isles and that, therefore, our climate cannot be modified by it, is negatived by a chart of the Gulf Stream just.issued by the Admiralty, The chart shows that the heated current is at all times found off Ireland and during a part of the year its waters lave the Irish coast.

div.head: OVERPOWERING PAIN.
div.p: OVERPOWERING PAIN.

To suffer excruciating torture for but a few moments is more than some people can stand. Our representa- tive, however, recently interviewed a man who had been on the rack of human misery for four months, and his story should prove useful to those who are interested in the sufferings our fellow mortals have to bear. "At first," he said, "I thought I had sprained my back, for suddenly T would be seized with a sharp stinging pain, which would creep, with cutting intensity, down from the shoulder blades, and then the small of my back would seem to be pierced by a dagger. So bad would Ibe that it was impossible for me to straighten myself up, and for several minutes I would have to remain almost bent in two. Sometimes sitting at breakfast the pain would come on me. It would then be only with the greatest difficulty that I could move away from the table, or even pick up the slightest weight. Many a night I have laid in agony, pierced by "excruciating pains. My urine was thick and cloudy, and of a colour to causeanxiety, and my health was breaking up under the strain it was called upon to bear. 'Moreover the amount' money spent upon numberless so-called positive cures, was a drain upon my scanty income that I could ill-afford. This, with the treatment I underwent at the hands of well-known local doctors, made me believe that a cure was out of the question. But I found re- lief through Dr. Morse's Indian Root Pills. A few bottles did for me what no other medicine could accom- plish ; my kidneys were put into a healthy state, my bladder was made strong, and once again I experienced all the joys of perfect health. They are a perfect blood purifier, curing eczema,pimples and blotches. Sold by leading chemists and stores, price is. 11d. per bottle.
