div.head: WARRINGTON WILL DISPUTE. Singular Action at the County Court.
div.p: WARRINGTON WILL DISPUTE. Singular Action at the County Court.
A WILL REVOKED.

An interesting case was heard at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C. respecting two wills which were made by the late Mrs. Mary Hollingworth, of Forster- street, Warrington. Mr. Hogg, barrister, Manchester, (instructed by Mr. Fowler solicitor), made an applica- tion on behalf of Ralph Hollingworth, tile merehant, 73, Knutsford-read, Warrington/ for a zevocation of a grant of probate of a will dated May 6th,. 1903 of Mary Hollingworth, deceased, and the granting of letters of administration of a subsequent will made on May 16th last. Mr. Hulton, barrister (instructed by Mr. Long- land, solicitor), opposed the application on behalf of Mary Wa!sh. Orford View, Winwick-road, and George Henry Darton, 52, Bewsey-street, the executrix and executor under the first will. Mr. Hogg, in opening the case, said the plaintiff was the oldest son and next of kin of the late MaryHolling- worth, who was about 80 years of age at the time of her death. Her last illness began about May Ist and her married daughter Mary Walsh went to live with her. On May 6th she had a will drawn up by Mr. Longland, solicitor, in which she left £2O and some household furniture to her grand-daughter, Ann Walsh; £5 to her son Frank Hollingworth; and the residue to her daughter, Mary Walsh, the mother of Ann Walsh and one of the defendants in the action. Ralph Honing.- worth. the plaintiff, paid daily visits to his mother during her illness and on May 13th, the latter had a foreboding that death was near and said to Ralph that she would like to leave all her children an equal share of the estate. Unknown to her daughter, Mary Walsh, a will was accordingly drawn up to that effect by a man named Frederick Massey. His Honour: The effect of the first will was to make Mary Walsh, the principal ben.eficiare,whereas under the , second will she was to share equally with the rest of the I 'children.

Mr. Hogg : That is so. On the 134:11 -Of May, the plaintiff took the will which had been drawn up by. Massey to his mother and read it over to her at her re- quest. She could not read or write and she asked whethor her name was on it. He replied " Yes at the bottom." She then told him to put it in the dress- ing-table drawer, saying "Don't tell Mrs. Walsh ; she will take it out and destroy it." Three days later Mr. Entwistle, a grandson, and his wife came over from Widnes to see her. She asked them to get the paper out of the dressing-table drawer and read it over to her. This was the will drawn up by Mr. Massey and having put her cross to it, Mr. and Mrs. Entwistle signed it as witnesses, and it was put in a sealedenvelope.

His Honour: Neither Mr. or Mrs. Entwistle are Ipneficiaries under the will? Mr. Hogg: No. The deceased lady told them not to say anything about it, but to put it in an envelope and take if away. This was on the 16th of May. Two days later another daughter of Mrs. Hollingworth came over to see her, and the old lady told her that she had arranged her money equally between all the children. On the 23rd of May she died. Ralph Hollingworth, the plaintiff, did not know whether the will which had been drawn up by Massey had been signed, because he was bound to secrecy to the old lady. Mr. and Mrs. Entwistle were equally bound, and they had not told the plaintiff what had taken place on the 16th of May. Mr. Dayton, who was one of the executors under the former will, asked the plaintiff for the keys and toldhim he could see the will at the solicitor's office. He and Entwistle went to the solicitor's office and found that by the will, Mrs. Walsh was the chief beneficiare. The plaintiff heard from the Entwistles of the existence of the later will which he had had drawn up and he delivered it sealed to Mr. Fowler, solicitor. Counsel pointed out that Ralph Hellingwo;th could not benefit by the will ashe was an undischarged bankrupt, and the money would have to go into the hands of the Official Receiver. An attempt had been made to get Holling- worth to swear that Mr. and Mrs. Entwistle were not in Warrington on the date of the will, but Hollingworth said he "was not going to tell lies for anybody." Frederick Shaw, record keener of the Liverpool pro- bate registry. produced the will of Mary Hollingworth, under date May 6th, 1903, and proved by Mary Walsh and George Henry Darton, the executors appointed by the will.

Ralph Hollingworth, tile merchant, Knutsford-road, eldest son of the testatrix, said Mrs. Hollingworth was ailing for two or three weeks before her deathand he went to see her continually. His sister, Mary Walsh, stayed with his mother daring her illness. One Wednes- day about ten days before she died he visited her. She said she did not think she would ever get better and she wanted to leave all her children equal shares of what she had. He asked her if she wished to make a will and she replied that she did. He said he did not understand how to draw one up but he would make inquiries. The same day hornet a Mr. Massey and told him than his mothor wanted to make a will. They both went to witness's office where Mr. Massey drew up the will on a piece of foolscap, leaving the date blank. In the evening witness went back to his mother's and told her he had got a will made out. She told him to put it it a drawer and she would have it witnessed in a day or two. She also asked him not to tell Mrs. Walsh about the will or she would destroy it. After his mother's death he searched for the will but could not find it After the funeral Mr. Darton asked him for the keys saying he was one of the executors appointed under a will made by Mrs. Hollingworth and witnessed by him several days before she died. He came to the conclu- sion that the will he had left in the drawer had been destroyed by Mrs. Walsh. He and Mr. Darton went to Mr. Longland's office where the first will was read over to them. On the 10th June he received a letter from his sister, Jane Entwistle,Widnes stating that her son had a will made by plaintiff' mother, which he and his wife had witnessed. That was the first intimation he had had that another wills had been signed. He went to Mrs. Entwistle who gave him a sealed envelope which he handed to Mr. Fowler, without opening. Mr. Fowler opened the envelope which contained thewill he had left in the drawer. On May 16th, Mr. Entwistle called and purchased some tiles from him. Witness did not benefit at all by the will.

Cross-examined: He had been adjudicated bank- rupt and had not yet obtained his discharge. A number of girls were employed at his mother's in the dressmaking business but they did not work in the bedrooni. Under the first will Mrs. Walsh and her daughter obtained the bulk of the property. When the first will was read out witness did not Mention that another had been drawn up. He thought his mother must have changed her mind since he saw her. At the funeral Mrs. Entwistle told him that his mother had left them all equal shares. Frederick Massey, 6, Gorsey lane, shipping clerk, de- posed to drawing up the will at the request of plaintiff. Ellen Entwistle, wife of William Entwistle, of Widnes said her husband was a "grandson of the testatrix. Witness came to Warrington with her husband on May 16th, the Saturday before Mrs. Hollingworth died. They went to see Mrs. Hollingworth who asked witness to take a paper out of a drawer in the dressing-table. The paper 'proved to be a will and witness read it over. Mrs. Hollingworth made a cross on the document and witness and her hus- band affixed their signatures, witness filling in the date. Mrs. Hollingworth then told her to put the will in an envelope, seal it up, keep it, and not 'breathe a word to anyone." William Entwistle, husband of the last witness, corro- borated. He denied having told anyone in a registry or insurance officethat his grandmother hal left no will. At this stage his Honour said he did not see how Mr. Hulton with the materials before him could hope to con- vince him that the second will was not properly executed._ _ _ .

Mr. Hulton said he could carry the case no further after his Honour'siobserva dons. His Honour thereupon granted the application. Some'argument ensued on the question of costs and his Honour directed them to be paid out of the estate •

div.head: DR. LUDWIG MOND.
div.p: DR. LUDWIG MOND.
Reported Dead but "Quite Well,"

Last Saturday a telegram reported that "Dr. Ludwig 'Mond, the distinguished chemist, died at Rome this morning" and several daily papers came out with a lengthy obituary notice, including the "Manchester Guardian" which published over half a column about the "late" doctor. The publication of the news created a feeling of much regret among the general public of Northwich, Winnington and surrounding districts, where the doctor is so well-known and highly respected; whilst among his many intimate friends, and those who have been long associated with him, upon whom the announcement came as a great surprise, the news caused keen distress. What the result must have been to the members of his family is difficult to des- cribe. The officials at Winnington works, the head- quarters of the world renowned chemical syndicate, as well as the residents of Winnington Hall, the Cheshire residence of the Mond family, tried throughout the day to obtain confirmation or denial of the report, but in this they were unsuccessful. It was known that Dr. and Mrs. Mond were in Switzerland, and not in Rome, and that the latest informa- tion to hand regarding his health was of a very hopeful character. These circumstances, com- bined with the fact that no distressing news had been received at either the London residences of Dr. Mond or Sir John Brunner, led to the report being discredited among tie principals engaged by the firm. The spirit of unrest, how- ever, was not altogether quieted until Sunday, morning, when a telegram was received at Winnington Hall, by Miss Handley, from St John's Wood, London. saying "Just received news from Cerisoli. Dr. Mond is well." This gladsome tiding was a sourse of great joy to those most inti- mately identified with the doctor. - -
A telegram dated Caux,Sunday,B.4o p.m.,was received from Dr. Mond himself saying, "Am perfectly well. Cannot understand how false report originated,"

div.head: CONFERENCE OF RECHABITES. Annual Gathering at Swansea.
div.p: CONFERENCE OF RECHABITES. Annual Gathering at Swansea.
TUESDAY

The High Movable Conference of the Independent Order of Rechabites was opened at Swansea on Tuesday delegates attending from all parts of the kingdom and from many of the colonies. rhe officers in attendance are H.C.R. Henry Wells-Smith, Sheffield; 11.D.R. Dun- can Kirkwood, Belfast; P.H.C.R. Andrew Bennett, Glasgow; H.S,J.T. Charles W. Churchill, Coreham ; H.T. Albert F. Briggs, Bradford; H.S. Richardson Cam- bell, Manchester; Director D. M. Main, Edinburgh; Director Robert Sheppard, Jarrow; Director Da,niel Thomas, Rhymuey ; Director John Sampson,Penzance ; Director LW. A. Platt, Bury; Director R. C. Griffin, Birmingham; Auditor D. M. Williams, Tonypandy ; Auditor Miles Taylor, Oldham ; Editor Henry Ward- ropper, P.H.C.R, ; Editor Y. W. Brett, P.H.C.R. Mr. W. Wright represented the Warrington district at the Con- ference.

The Mayor of Swansea (Mr. Griffith Thomas)officially welcomed the delegates on Monday night, and the btthiness of the Conference opened on Tuesday morning. The Reception Committee, headed by their chairman Brother J. Rosser, presented to the H.C.R. a specially bound record of temperance work in the district as a souvenir of the visit to Swansea.

The High Chief Ruler then delivered his presidential address, in the course of which he said that, on many occasions extending over many years, difficulties had arisen with influential initiates as to the literal meaning of their pledge. In some cases the ceremony had been abruptly terminated • in others the spirit and intention and not the words of the pledge had been subscribed to. There were other circumstances in which the loyalty of the truest of their friends had been severely shaken. The covenant of total abstinencelthe separation from sale, manufacture, and social and business treating must be upheld and, if necessary, fought for, but a broad, tolerant interpretation was needed if the words dealing with the other matters remained as at present. He suggested the following revised version of the pledge :—"I hereby pledge myself to the principles and practice of total abstinence from all intoxicating liquors as beverages, including British and foreign fermented wines. I declare that, excepting at religious ordinances or in times of sickness or other special circumstances (and then only after reflecti9n upon my duty as a Rechabite) I will not use intoxicants or give or offer them to others. I will not either as principal, partner, shareholder, or as a free agent engage in the traffic in intoxicating drinks, but will in all commendable ways discountenance the use, manufacture, and sale of them and the baneful custom of tolerating the same at trade or social functions or at political, athletic, or like institu- tions of which I may at any time be a member." They were an old, and great and perhaps the oldest and great- est, total abstinence Society whose members subscribed to a common pledge and recognized one person as the official head and authority. He thought they were des- tined ere long to be the greatest among the affiliated Orders with branches and holding regular meetings. That they were the best already few would dare. dispute. The officers and executive members expressed the opinion that they were not accorded their proper place in the ranks of the national bodies, perhaps owing to the fact that some of the smaller societies had persons at their head who had been there for ceveral years, which they as Rechabites, owing to the more satisfactory dis- tribution of honours and service, could not have. In this connection they had a proposal to appoint an organising agent, as to the wisdom of which they were the judges; but it became more and more apparent to him that their success in gaining and keeping status in the indicated quarters, in making and shaping bills for i Parliament, n vitalising their principles and making them operative with the men in the street would depend to a large extent upon their having a Parliamentary agent, as was the case with the Oddfellows, Foresters, and United Kingdom Alliance, and as was proposed by National Conference of Friendly Societies. Brother Story, of Birmingham, initiated a discussion on an alteration in the declaration of members by which it was propsed to add: "I will not become a share- holder of a club or institute where intoxicating liquors are sola."—Brother Hardy (Northumberland seconded. Brother Clark (Cumberland) asked for leave to amend by adding the word "knowlngly."—On a vote being taken leave was granted.—The opposition was led by Brother S. A. Scarlett and Brothers Commode and Stanton, of Northumberland, who contended that the matter was already covered by the pledge.—On the sug- gestion of Brother Wardropper it was agreed that the Durham representatives should meet the Business Committee and bring up a resolution for submission again to the Conference.

-The Credential Committee at this stage reported that the total attendance, including high officers, was 176. Of representatives there were 156, including four colonials. It was agreed, on the motion of &other Thompson, of Lincoln, seconded by Brother Scarlett, of Norfolk, to add to the objects of the Society "paying members' contributions after they reach the age of 60 years." Motions from South Wilts and Sheffi.eld pro- posing that past chief rulers should have a seat with voting powers at the Conference was negatived by a great majority. By a card vote of 168 to 154 on the proposal of the Edinburgh district, it was decided that "no district shall have more than one member serving on the board of directors, but the office of High Secre- tary shall not come under the provision of the rule." 'The Conference adjourned. WEDNESDAY. .

The business of the fortieth High Movable Confer- ence of the Independent Order of Rechabites was re- sumed at the Albert Hall,Swansea,on Wednesdavjmorning. The first business was the consideration of the report of the Board of Directors, which showed that the pro- gress of the Order had been remarkable, notwithstand- ing the limitations imposed by the pledge of abstinence The net increase of 34,760 adult and juvenile benefit members in two years bore comparison with any other results in the friendly society world. The funds on January Ist. 1902, stood at £1,227,116, the income last year was £332,064, and the benefits paid amounted to £196,642. The total membership was 303,777. ' In the course of a discussion on the consolidation of , districts, Bro. Phillipson of Northunaberland, showed Ithat the number of Reckabites to population in the kingdom was one in 163. Scotland, which was consoli- dated, showed one in 77, Northumberland district one in 59, and Durham (non-consolidated) one in 85. The question was whether they could, as they ought to do, bring the number to population to one in 50. He thdught this could be the better done by consolidation. The report of Bro. Churchill, H.S.J.T., showed that the increase of juvenile membership amounted to 16,798 exceeding by 4,000 the largest increase ever previously reported. Eight thousand members had been transferred to the adult section in the same period. The juvenile membership in the home districts amounted to 100,000. The colonial districts had contributed2,ll3 towards the increase. It was decided specially to recognize the work of the Heywood district, which won the national challenge shield in 1901 by an increase of over 40 per cent andketained it in 1902 by an inezease of 69 per cent. With regard to old-age pensions, the directors report stated :—" We think friendly societies would be more usefully occupied in arranging the pensions for their own members at 60 or 65 years of age on the lines em- bodied in our general rules some years ago, and of making it compulsory on all new entrants, after a given period, to pay for sickness benefits terminating at the appointed age' and superannuation benefits beyond that age, and towards this end we recommend that the incoming Board be empowered to communicate withthe National Conference of Friendly Societies and its con- stituent orders and societies, suggesting that all such orders or societies assuring benefits such as our Order does, bind themselves to adopt this course of action, to operate as and from January 1, 1910, or earlier by arrangement. State aid and voluntary thrift are apart and distinct, and we strongly advise our membership to keep the two questions separate, and from a friendly society point of view to entrench the grand principle of self-help and mutual brotherhood,and as citizens to require the State to do justice to the aged deserving poor." The relief fund showed one farthing per member per annum had more than sufficed for all approved claims. The amount paid since the last A.M.C. to the 13 tents was £267, compared with £577 reported six years ago. Brother John Parry, Abergavenny, desired to add to the declaration of the directors with regard to vested interests in licences, but this suggestion was not accepted. The directors declared it to be the duty of IRechabites to effect a clearance of drinking dens at any cost, but not to allow the pretence of compensation by ; either of the bills before Parliament to lead them from Ithe main line of attack.
The directors' report was adopted, and the Confer- ence again adjourned. THURSDAY.

The session was resumed on Thursday at the Albert Hall, Swansea. Brother Wells Smith presiding. It was decided, on the motion of Brother Lord, seconded by Bro. Brown, Manchester, to accept females transferred from juvenile tents at half the usual district management levy. In the case of a member's wife's death it was agreed that a sum up to £2O be paid instead of £lO. An amendment from the Northumberland district was carried by which a member may now insure, in the funeral fund only. In a discussion on a proposal to allow districts to insure member's for continuous half- sick pay Brother Joynes, North Midland, opposed the proposal, asserting that minerSwere really getting bene- fit that they ought not to have, and that they (Recha- bites) had a difficulty on account of the high rates of benefits. The proposal, however, was agreed to. Brother Churchill, H.S.T.J., moved and Brother Tourton (Nottingham) seconded the adoption of the following declaration, which was submitted by a com- mittee of the Conference to which the matter had been referred :—" The High Movable COnference declares that it is a violation of the pledge of the Order thut member should be connected with a profit-sharing club or institute where intoxicating liquors are sold." This was unanimously carried. It was decided, on the recommendation of. the Board of Directors, that the various I.istricts of the United Kingdom shall be arranged into provinces for the 'pur- pose of holding juvenile provincial conferences when approved by the Juvenile Comraittee and the Board of Directors ; also that a new office be established in con- nection with the district assistant superintendent of

Juvenile Templars. It Was also decided that in the event of a district having any surplus funds a portioi of the same may be used to pay part of contribution of a member on being transferred, provided such member has been one or two years in a juvenile tent. Brother D. M. Moyne, director, presented the asses meat report bearing upon the requirements of the n_e, . two years. He stated that increased expenditure haa been created by additions to the number of directorg, and this was met by an increase in the management deputational and valuation levy. With regard to relief levi the Committee thought the balance in that fund, viz,' £l.ooo was ample as a reserve, and inastaueu as the claims for relief are diminishing they ree°lll" mended the reduction of that levy to the point of one- eighth of a penny per annum. They also recommended that the juvenile levy be continued as at present--4d• per member per annum. After luncheon the election of officers was proceeded with. Brother Wells Smith moved that Brother Kirk- wood be elected High Chief Ruler. This was carried with acclamation.. Brother Churchill (North Wilts) vittS elected Deputy High Chief Ruler. The Conference adjourned till the following day.

HOLLOWAY'S PROTECTED.—In the recent 'act i 0 Holloway V. Cleat, Mr. Justice Swinfen Eady, in the Chancery Division made perpetual an interim injunction recently granted by him restraining the defendant from using the name " Holloway "in connection with pills and ointment sold by him. At the first hearing of the case his lordship, in/granting the injunction, remarked thation the facts alleged by the plaintiff, it appeared to be *use of " gross fraud." At the final hearing on July 29th, his lordship was satisfied of the justice of the plaintiff's case, and therefore granted a perpetual injunction with costs. Mr. Israel Davies appeared for the plaintiff ; Mr. Jessel for the - defendant. The suc- cessful party in this fsuit is, of course, Thomas Holloway, proprietor of the well-known Holloway's Pills and Ointment.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday August 8, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday August 8, 1903.
TWO DROWNING FATALITIES.
SINGULAR DEATH OF A STOCKTON HEATH CARTER,
The Viewing of Bodies.

Mr. J. H. Fisher, deputy coroner, conducted an in- quiry at the Red Lion Hotel, Stockton Heath, on Tuesday morning, relative to the death of Herbert Kendrick Sykes, aged 28, who resided in Gaskell-street, Stockton Heath, and whose body was recovered from the river at the rear of Messrs. Greenall Whitley and Company's stables at Wilderspool. The deceased was engaged in the delivery of bottled beer and stout for the company,and on returning to the brewery on Thurs- day afternoon last week he appeared in his usually cheerful mood. He remarked, however, to Mr. E. Lawton, the foreman bottler, that he did not feel "over grand" and would leave another load which he had to take until the following day. This was at about a quarterto five, and as far as can be gathered, he was not seen aliveagam. Dragging operations were conducted on Saturday, and about 7.30 p.m., Francis Bottles, a bridgeman in the employ of the Manchester Ship Canal Company recovered the body from the river behind the company's stables. The first witness called was

Robert Holmes, 128, Greenall's-avenue, a carter in the employ of the company. He stated that he saw the deceased close to the brewery at 4.30 on Thursday. Sykes wasa man of temperate habits and cheerful dis- position. Sykes and his wife lived together" like boy and girl," hislaccounts were straight at the Brewery,and there was not the slightest indication that Sykes would make away with himself. Thomas Pierpoint, 33, Walton-road, painter,said Sykes was well when he saw him at 4.30 at the Brewery. He asked Sykes if he had finished, and received the reply: "No, not quite; I have ray horses and harness to do." They both walked down the drive together from the offioe to the main road. Sykes had his coat off and sleeves rolled up, and witness observed "You look ready for a couple of rounds." Sykes made a jocular reply, and witness then left him by the fire station. The deceased seemed in good health and spirits. Witness had never heard him complain about any unhappiness. He was very much surprised to hear on Friday night that Sykes was missing, because he was such a jolly man.—By Sergeant Barlow: There was a road leading from the Brewery yard to the river. When witness left the deceased he was going towards the stable.—By Mr. Whitley: Some of the Brewery men were in the habit of going down by the riverside. vom

Piannis Beetles, 20, Gaskell-street, Stockton Heath bridgeman in the employ of the Ship Canal Company spoke to recovering the body at 7.30 on Saturday night from the river at the rear of the Brewery, after grap- pling from 5.30. The body was dressed, but deceased had not got his coat on, while his sleeves were rolled up. There were no marks of violence on the body.—By Sergeant Barlow: At about 4.30 on Thursday the river at the point in question would be some 14 feet deep, the tide being in. The water would be level with the bank.

Edwin Lawton. 10, Green Bank, Wilderpool, foreman bottler, said he had known the deceased for many years. He last saw him alive about a quarter to five on Thursday afternoon. He remarked to witness that he was not feeling overweli and that he would take his next load on the following morning. Witness agreed to this and deceased then went to put his horse in the stable. The deceased was a very good servant of the company and the firm regretted having lost his services. He was thoroughly honest and trustworthy and his accounts Were perfectly straight. He was not a man whom one would think likely to take his own life. There was no reason for the deceased to go through the stable yard to the river bank.
The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned." A ro MR. WHITLEY RAISES AN IMPORTANT QUESTION.

At the close of the inquiry, Mr. Whitley, the foreman of the jury, pointed out that the expenses of inquests were paid out of a county rate met by the overseers and averaged £5 for each inquest. There was an impost at Stockton Heath last month and considering the increase of population if inquests continued at the present rate there would be twelve in a year. This would mean an. expenditure of 60 out of the rates. In the present case the body of the deceased was found in the borough of Warrington and brought into the parish of Stockton Heath where the inquest had to be held. He asked which county would be charged with the expenses. The Deputy-Coroner said the cost would have to be met by Cheshire.

Mr. Whitley then asked if it was imperative for juries to view the body on the occasion of each inquest. The deceased was missed six days ago and the body was in such an advanced state of decomposition when recovered that lt, was totally unfit to be viewed and was unrecognizable. The oeffui had alr.adv 13.011 oloand for health and sanitary reasons. Mr. Whitley gave an instance of a body being recovered from the Ship Canal and it was in such a shocking state that several jury- men became ill.
The Deputy Coroner remarked that it was very re- grettable. Mr. Whitley added that the viewing of bodies did not add oue iota of evidence as to how deceased met his death.
• The Deputy Coroner said it was made compulsory by the law for jurymen to view bodies. Mr. Whitley said the law was a farce in such cases as he had mentioned.
The Deputy Coroner said he could nothelp that. They were just as much bound to view the body as they were to pay the education rate.

div.head: SAD DROWNING CASE AT BEWSEY. "They wont see Jack France Again."
div.p: SAD DROWNING CASE AT BEWSEY. "They wont see Jack France Again."

lir. Brighouse, County Coroner' conducted an inquiry at Sankey Chapel House, Great Sankey, on Wednesday evening, respecting the death of John France,a puddler, of 2, Ellis-street, Warrington, whose body was picked out of the Liverpool and St. Helens Canal at Bewsey on Sunday morning. He had been misting from his horae since the previous Tuesday evening. Jane France, wife of the deceased, said her husband was 46 years of age. He come home from his work on Tuesday night last week (July 28th) at six o'clock. He gave her half-a-crown and left home at seven o'clock. She met him a little later at Bewsey Bridge and he said "I will go to Jack Worrall's and have a pint there." She re- turned home at 7.30 but her husband did not come home until after ten o'clock. He was then under the influence of drink and he quarreled with her. She did not see him leave the house.,

Mrs. Elizabeth tuner, who lived with the last witness, said she recollected the deceased coming home at 10.20 on the night in question. The deceased quarreled with his wife and then went upstairs. He came down again, partly dressed, and witness put him out because he was quarreling. She afterwards gave the deceased his clogs, coat and vest but she would not allow him in the house again. He then went away. P. C. Houghton, of the Warrington Borough Police Force, stated that he was on duty in Hoyle street and saw the deceased at the back door of number 2, Ellis street. The deceased wanted to gain admittance, but the last witness (Elizabeth Trynar) would not let him in. She would not even givehim his clothes. Witness interposed and asked her how she could expect the man to go away in his bare feet. She then gave the deceased his clogs, coat and vest and he went away. The deceased said his wife and children were there, and added "they wont see Jack France again." George Howell, of 25, Pierpoint street, a striker, stated that he was standing at the canal bridge at Bewsey on Sunday morning, about a quarter past eleven o'clock, when he saw some flats passing along the canal towards St. Helens. Imme- diately afterwards he saw a body come to the surface of the water. Witness got a boat hook and took the body out of the water. He then sent for the police. P.C. Dugdale stated that he received the body from the last witness. There were no marks of violence upon it and it Appeared to have been inthe water four or five days. He found a pair ef spectacles two hair pins and a tobacco pipe in the pockets. The jury returned a verdict of" Found Drowned."

div.head: Ambulance Work on the Great Central Rail-
div.p: Ambulance Work on the Great Central Rail-
way.

An interesting presentation took place on the 31st July at London-road Station by Colonel Royds C. 8., M.P. one of the directors of the Great Central. Rai- lway 'Company. Colonel Royds a little time ago pre- sented a shield for competition, which has been won by the Hull Ambulance , Team, and will be held at Hull for one year. The shield is of beautiful design and the names of the men of the Hull Team have been engraved thereon. The captain of the team is Mr. R. W. Winter, and the other four members . are Messrs, Cuthbert, Lord, Smith and Foster. The winning of the shield also carries with it a in -ney prize of £5. Colonel Royds in pre- senting the shield to the team complimented the men on the efficiency which they had attained, and com- mented. on the humane work. performed by Ambulance men in relieving their fellow sufferers. In connection with the Competition the Newton Team were adjudged second and won a money prize of £3, and the Penis- tone Team were third, winning a prize of £2. Unfor- tunately the General Manager of the Company (Mr. Fa-), was unable to be present, but the following Officers attended.--:-Mr. R. Haig Browne, Mr. C, W. Neele, Mr. .0. T. Smith, Mr. AV. Clow, Mr. C. A. RowlandsOn, Mr. J. W. Lee, Mr. 0. S. Holt, Mr. A. Furniss, Mr. J. Rostern, Mr. W. Edge, Mr. J. Pollard the Company's Ambulance Secretary.

div.head: SWIMMING.
div.p: SWIMMING.
MILE CHAMPIONSHIP OF/ENGLAND.

Only three competitors contested the mile champion- ship of England at Leicester on Tuesday Jarvis (the holder) did not compete. Billington (Bacup) speedily assumed the lead, and was never seriously troubled by the other competitors—Law (Cha,dderton) and Short- house (Salford)—steadily increasing his lead with every, turn. He completed half the distance in 12min. 19sec.1 He appeared to tire slightly towards the close, but completed the distance in 24min. 5G 2-ssec.-17see inside the weed's record. Law second, 200 yard: behind.

div.head: NEW HOSPITAL FOR LIVERPOOL.
div.p: NEW HOSPITAL FOR LIVERPOOL.

Liverpool Corporation on Wednesday decided to btild a new hospital for infectious diseases at Fazakerlev, for £121,457, plus £40,000 for the land and £s,ooofCir furniture; the hospital to accommodate from 30) to 350 patients, at an annual cost of £15,000. Aid. (Dr.) Clarke said that Glasgow and Edinbirgh had built hospitals at a cost of £650 per head; at Liverpool the cost woull be £5OO per head. Messrs, Morrison and Sons, Wavertree, are the oontracton. It wasreported at Stockport Town Council on Wed- nesday that during the small-pox epidemic the Sani- tary Committee, to induce lodging-house frequenters to be vaccinated, agreed to pay seven days' lodgings for every person vaccinated. As a result the nedical officer vaccinated 4:12 persons.

Partington was found to besuffering from delirium tremens, and the tragedy was a myth. The man was sent to the Workhouse on Thursday. BANK HOLIDAY AT Si. HELENS. div.head: MUNICIPAL TRADING,
div.p: MUNICIPAL TRADING,
MR. NORBURY WILLIAMS INTERVIEWED.
CRITICISM OF THE PARLIAMENTARY JOINT COMMITTEE'S REPORT.

div.head: Abolition of the Elective Auditor.
div.p: The Abolition of the Elective Auditor.
STRONG CONDEMNATION.

A representative of the " Examiner " yesterday inter- viewed Mr.S. No rbury Williams,the well-known Manches- ter elective auditor,in order to ascertain his opinions on the report issued this week by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Municipal Trading. The report deals verylargely with the auditing of the accounts of public bodies, and recommends an entire change involving the abolition of elective auditors. Instead it is proposed that professional accountants should be appointed auditors by the local bodies, subject to the Local Government Board's approval. It was this suggested vital change in the system of municipal Government that the interviewer sought expert opinion upon. In answer to aprelimirutry question Mr. WILLIAMS said: "I hold the view I have always held that there can be no objection whatever to the appointment of a fully-qualified accountant to inspect and audit the accounts of the great Corporations but I do object,and shall continue to object to the move that is now being made on the recommendation of the Joint Select Committee on Municipal Trading to abolish the office of elective auditor. What I insist upon is that the ratepayers must have a direct representative who shall have full access to the accounts of the Corpora- tion and who can be at any time consulted by individual ratepayers."
"You are iaopposition to the Select Committee ,then?' queried the reporter.

"In my opinion the Select Committee has not formed a correct view of the present condition of affairs. In clause 16a of their report they expressly propose that,`The existing systems of audit applicable to Corporations, ICounty Councils and Urban District Councils in lEngland and Wales be abolished.' The following im portent passage also occurs in their recommendations: 'The lelective auditors are poorly paid, or are unpaid altogether, little interest is taken in their election, and although in some cases they are able to layra linger on a particular irregularity Ms not clear that they could not make the same discovery ia the capacity of active rate- payers. No complete or continuous audit is ever attempted by them."

"In this respect, the Joint Committee have made an entire mistake. They don't appear to understand the true condition of affairs in reference to individual rate- payers and the inspection of the accounts of Corpora- tions. They have not grasped the difference between theoxisting condition of things and the new condition which they propose to institute. At present, and for 70 years past, the individual ratepayer has through his own representative--the elective auditor—had access to the accounts of his own Council, but under the pro- posed new condition of things this most salutary pro - vision will be abolished. It is to ma both amusing and interesting to see the easy way in which the Select Comniittee waveaside the old representative and bring in the new one."
"Do you in any way attribute the attitude of the Committee to outside influence ?"

"The Association of Municipal Corporations has, I believe, long been working with a view to abolish elec- tive auditors and the result of this working is now plainly seen in the recommendations of the Joint Com- mittee. I have no objection whatever, as I have said before and have frequently said publicly and even said to the Joint Committee, to the appointment of pro- fessional accountants to audit the accounts of the Cor- poration but I have said danitely and I say now with redoubled force that if the burgesses of England permit theabolition of the office of elective auditor they will be more helpless than ever in dealing with the financial undertakings of their own Cor- porations. Their condition will in fact be pitiable. One need only refer to my own city of Manchester. For 20 years men of the most entire competence in accountancy have audited our accounts. They have had under their view no fewer than one million invoices during that period. To not one of that vast number have they raised any objection. Yet in that time great scandals havearisen. Much wrong-doing has taken place. Many illegal payments have been made. Yet the professional auditors have remained silent. The new condition of things will be the same under this lamentable recommendation of the Joint Parliamentary Committte.Men of the same calibre will be selected and what is worse they will be selected by the men whose accounts they will have to audit. This is the radical defect of the recommendation." "Severe criticism, Mr. Williams?"

"Yes, it is, but I think I can justify it. At present the burgesses elect the auditor, under the new condition of things the men who expend the money will nominate their own auditor. Our last condition will be worse than the first. One need only take the case of Warring- ton at this moment. The condition of sentiment in the town is well-known and yet if the recommendations of the Joint Committee were now in force,the Warrington Town Council would select one quality of man, while the burgesses would undoubtedly select a man of an entirely different sort." "Judging by recent events I should believe that to be true," commented the interviewer.

Continuing Mr. Williams added: "At present the professionalauditors in our own city of Manchester are appointed for a period not exceeding three years but in the coarse of my evidence I suggested this might possibly be extended to five years. I note now that the Joint Committee is suggesting practically that the term of office of an auditor may go on for an indefinite time. Clause 16c says 'ln every case the appointment should be subject to the approval of the Local Government Board after hearing any objections made by ratepayers, and the auditor who should hold office fora term not exceed- ing five years should be eligible for re-appointment and should not be dismissed by the local authority without the sanction of the Board.' This means that a firm may obtain an auditorship and hold it to the end of the chapter. This in my opinion is exceedingly objection- able and the present arrangement in Manchester is much preferable."
"The elective anditor is absolutely necessary then, from many points of view?"

"It is of vital importance to the burgeizes that they should have their own auditor, elected cul hoc,and unless this is given when a bill is introducedinto Parliament— if it should be introduced on the recommendationof the Joint Committee—it will be necessary for the burgesses to take joint action to secure that in future, as in the past, one or more definite direct representatives of the burgesses shall be electeg who shall have the power and the right to investigate every figure in connection with Corporation expenditure."
"Under the suggested new system of audit, do you think there would be still less information vouchsafed In regard to Corporation accounts?"

1 "The public are aware at present of the obstacles placed in the way of those parties who desire access to the minutes of their own Corporation. I again insist that every obstacle is placed in their way. If we quietly sit down and allow the office of elective auditor to be abolished we shall be more in the dark than ever and as burgessses we shall deserve all we get. The professional accountants even under the new order of things would be paid a stipulated sum by the Council appointing them. As a matter of mere commercialism these professional accountants would say it was im- possible to pursue such inquires as really ought to be pursued. They would look on the amount of their remu- neration and would naturally only put in such a quantity of time as was paid for. I have not the smallest doubt that under the new order of things a large number of illicit payments would be made and which are still being made at this moment in probably nine-tenths of the Corporations in the country. It is more than over necessary,. seeing the great expenditure in connection withiMunlcipal Trading that the one office which gives the burgesses a direct ascess through their representative to the accounts of their own Corporation shall not be abolishei, but on the other hand strengthened." With this final firm opinion from Mr. Williams, the interview closed, and the reporter hurried off to trans- cribe the valuable information he had, through Mr. Williams' courtesy, been able to glean.

div.head: [BY 511 WILLIAM fiIiTUOURTa
div.p: [BY 511 WILLIAM fiIiTUOURTa

-We are told that we are "threatent=d " • (that i the phrase of the Duke of Devonshire) with a 'discussion next October which has for its object to reverse the policy of Free Trade, under which this nation has grown, and is growing still, in the .prosperity, wealth, and contentment Of the people. It is za remarkable,zir_ cumstance that this "threat" shotild proceed frow a colleague of the Duke who is like a•'veileti prophet,' to propound, at his own convenience, sto the nation a plan for which be has not obtained the assent either of the Government or the party to which be balongs. He has told us mighty lktle about hs plan except that it is to tax the food of the people of the United Kingdom in order to secure-the loyalty of the British. Colonies. The object aimed ft is superflu- ous, and the means proposed are mischievous. The Colonies are as loyal as anyone could desixe, and they have shewn it by deeds even beyond our hopes. What is the pretence, therefore, for an attempt to revolution- ise our whole fiscal fsyStem, to establish a protective tariff, and to disturb oar vast trade with the world? It is said that we must • bind the Colonies to ILS by ties of interest. At present they are united to us by bonds of brotherhood, of pride

and of affection. They ;have shown 'how ready they were to shed their blood for us in our difficulties. But this is not enough for Mr. Chamberlain. We must be united lsy obligatioas of "interest" or the Empire : will be lost.. We must bargain for preferential tariffs And the inOspensable eondition of preferential tariffs, is, he informs us, taxation of the food of our people, and probably of the raw material of our manufactures, That, as the Duke jastly calls it, is a threatening challenge. If it is to be dealt with as a question of "interest," I i.suppose it meals the "interest" of both parties. If we are to deal ,with the Colonies on a footing of bargain and sale we must inquire. How does the balance of interests stand? With his accustomed frankness and good sense the Duke of Devonshirehas put the practical issue plain and straight in his speech to the Empire • 11.eague : _

Englishmen boast that they are a plain-spoken race; and I do not think that the least plain-spoken afnong the British race are those that dwell in our Colonies—(laughter)—and I think it would be well that -we should both speak to each other on this great,subject in the plainegt possible terms. We are bound to let the Colonies know that this question has.reached a stage—that this question, which was starte.d as a Colonial one, has reached a stage almost -at its very inception—in which it has become far more-, a question of internal British politics than -even. of Colonial politics. I am sure that our Colonial countrymen will not resent it if we make 'them .understand, as I think in honesty we are bound •to make them understand, that this question has -reached a practical and is no longer in a senti- mental stage. Sentiment and business are each very good things, but I do not think that much -advantage is derived from attempting to mix ' them up together. It is sentiment which binds the family together. It is sentiment which induces /every member of a family to come to the rescue and assistance of any other member who may be in difficulty or distress •, and it is similar sentiment which does, and I think always will, chiefly bind our Colonies to the Mother Country. But Ido not know that very much advantage is fotmdWhen mem- -hers of a family who have set up for themselves in business attempt to conduct that business with , their parents or with each other on purely -senti- mental principles. If we keep in view, as we are always bound to keep in view, as our first object I the maintenance, strength, and prosperity of this great Empire, the cardinal, the first question, which an Imperial statesman has to consider is the strength, prosperity, and welfare of the centre; and I am sure the Colonists will not resent it if we tell them plainlyand clearly that if we are induced to assent to any considerable changes in our fiscal and commercial arrangements, which we have hitherto thought conducive to our interests, we shall do it in our own interest, and not simply for the purpose or as a means of conciliating their goodwill. It is well that this matter should be emphatically stated—that the cardinal, the first question which an im- peria/ statesman .has to consider is the strength and prosperity and welfare of the centre of the Empire, and that if we mak,e any changes in our fiscal system weshal do it in our own interests, and not simply as a means of conciliating the goodwill of the Colonies. Let us 'consider, then, shat are the benefits we confer upon the Colonies, and what are those we derive from them? We undertake from the oppressive taxation of our people practically the whole burthen of the defence of the Colonies. Mr.

Chamberlain stated to the Conference last year that "the charge of our military and naval expenditure amounted to 295. 3d. per head of the population of the United Kingdom,and in the self-governing Colonies it amounted to sums varying from 25.. to 3s. sd. He asked whether that was a fair distribution of the burthen of empire. Could it be expected that the United Kingdom could for all time make this inordinate sacrifice? It is owing to its duties and obligations to its Colonies throughout the Empire,it is owing to its trade with these Colonies —a trade in which they,of course,are equally interested with ourselves—that the necessity has been cast upon us to make these enormous preparations." As the result of ,the Cenference certain small contribu- tions were agreed to, amounting in the whole to a sum , which •Scl not•greatlralter the enormous disproportionl of burthen as between the Mother Country and the ' Colonies. On this head,therefore,there can be no ques- tion that in the balanced "interests" the Colonies have immensely the advantage. Let us see how the matter stands on the balance of trade and commerce. We have given to Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, and the Cape and Natal, an autonomy which does not belong to India and the Crown Colonien—the absolute right to deal with their taxation and tariffs as they think fit in their own interests. We give 'them a free market for all their produce and manufactures, and we are their best customers. They, on the other hand, have placed heavy duties on our exports to them, partly for revenue and partly to protect their ,own industries. Here again the balance of interest is heavily on their side, and to our disa lvantage. What, then, is jt pre Posed sbould be done' in order to bind the Mother Country and Colonies by ties of mutual interest? Is it to equalise the 'burthens as between the two parties? On the contrary, the 'first demand propounded by Mr. Chamberlain is that a further sacrifice shall be made by imposing a tax on the food of the people of the United Kingdom, and pretty certainly on the raw materials of their mannfacturem. Our burthens, therefore, already too great, are -to be aggravated by taxation of the most odious and the most unequal character. The Colonies are to impose no new taxes, they are only to remit them. Whilst our food is to be taxed theirs will be free. Is that dealing fairly by the "centre of the Empire"? What is, then. held out on the other ..side to redress the balance? Nothing but a vague suggestion of a reduction in favour of British trade of a certain fraction of the heavy duties now leviedin the Colonies upon it. What is to be the amount of that reduction, and what Will be its value? That we are not told. We are informed that at the Conferencalast year "the Prime Ministers of the Colonies undertook to submit to their Governments the principle of preferential tariffs, and to request them to seek occasions to give effect to it: Though we are told expressly that we are to put a tax upon food, we are not informed what the Coloniat Governments are on their part to give us iu exchange We are told it is to be a reduction of their hostile tariffs against British trade. More than a year has passed, and we have no definite information on the sub. ject. In the report of the Conference we read (p. 3) : " Australia : Preferential treatment not yet defined as to nature or extent; Now Zealand: A general pre- ference of 10 per cent. ; Cape and Natal: prefer- ence of 25 per cent." We may form some judgment as to the value of such concessions by the outcome of the grant of a prefer- ence of 33 per cent, by Canada five years ago. The history of this matter is deserving of close attention. Mr. Chamberlain says in his report of the Conference jast per (p. 7): In M 7 the Premiers of the Colonies unanimously undertook to consult with their colleagues, and to pcittsider whether .preferetkce ptiettt not be given in

!theirliustbmis "Itirifig tcr goods imported from the PREFERENTIAL 'DUTIES. Unite'd Kingdom. -Tiat;lt a proposal Without resipnocal iolAigabious. was was regarded by the Premiers at the tianeas a proposal which, might be wide in consideratiomef the fact that the United THE MOTE ER COUNTRY AND 'THE Kingdom. was the *trgest, the best, and the most 'open anarket in the -.world for the products of the COLONIES. Goionies. But nothingthas come of the resolution up to-the present time. No step has been taken to give.enect to it. This is the most important statement in its bearing I"an thepre.sent 'discussion. 'Mr. Chamberlain and all the , Colonial Premiers were oftipirion that a preferenceehotild ,be given by the Colonies in their Custom Tariffs for 'god& imported from the United , Kingdom, and that without any reciprocal obligation, the equivalent being already supplied by the free access in the United King- dom for all the Colonial trkcie. , What has happened to alter that .situation? Why, now, is the "reciprocal obligation*" put forward, in the shape of a deemnd for • the taxation of the food of the people or the United Kingdom, which -was then expressly disclagirned ? i What has happened in Canada is very instructive as showing the practical valueOf such a conceersion by way of preference in the Colonies. The Canadtian Govern- ment granted a preference,ef 33 per cent; on British taxable goods imported into the Dominiont. ;Laurier stated that at ;the time it v‘ tits volun- tarily given, without asking any return, in con Isideration 'of the free access to the British market of! Canadian produce, and no equivalent was asked or expe civet ; and it was expressly stated that there was "no id 'ea of ask- ing the Mother Country to depart from the F see Trade from whichshe had ilerived such advantage." at has liseen the practical result of this preference , eif :never .eent in Canada? Mr. Chamberlain, in the Repo. oof Conference, 1962, says (p. 7) : The time that has elapsed has been suffi tient to, enable us to form a judgment of the effect of an arrangement of this kind, and I have to say -Ito you that while T cannot but gratefully acknowle 4Ae the intention of this proposal, and its sentiment 2 Lel as a proof of goodwill and affection, yet th rat it- substantial results have been altogether dim' Opsint--, ing to us, and I think they must have been e disappointing to the promoters- . . The total! increase of the trade in Canada with forei 'cners'l daring the period named, that is, including bot ;kith°, trade subject to the tariff, and also the free t was 69 per cent. whilst the total increase of 131 'lash; trade was only ,18 per cent. . . . The net re snit,i I desire to impress upon yon, is, t in /spite of the preference which Canada lasi given us, their tariff has pressed, still presses, with the greatest severity . upon lbsi best customers, and has favoured the formgner.w is constaatly doing his best to shut out her gooc Ts. . . . We may most readily and most gratefull accept from you any preference which you may b, willing voluntarily to accord to us. We cesnno,tl bargain with you for it.. We cannot pay for it ; unless you go much further, and enable us to enter your home markets on terms of greater equality. So long as is preferential tariff, even a munificent, preference, is sufficiently protective to exclude us altogether, or nearly so, from your markets, it is no satisfaction to us that you have imposed even greater disability upon the same goods if they come from foreign markets. What assurance is here offered—l might say what probability is there—that any such preference will be accorded by the Colonies? They have made up their minds to protect their own manufactures by sufficient duties to prevent effective competition with them by British no less than foreign traders ;and at this moment Australia is contemplating, like Cenada,adding bounties to protective tariffs to preserve her own interests against all intruders. On a review of the balance of interests which Mr. Chamberlain invites us to consider, it is plain that the enormous preponderance is at present in favour of the Colonies. The demand, therefore, that we should under- take to place additional burthens upon the people of the United Kingdom is altogether unreasonable and unfair. To attempt to enforce what Mr. Cnamberlain has himself designated as a "one-sided bargain" is acourse which will not unite but disturb the Empire. In a dithyrambic outburst of patriotic pathos Mr. Chamberlain ejaculated to the admiring Colonial Conference, " The weary Titan staggers under the too vast orb of its fate. We have borne the burden for many years. We think it is time that our children should assist us to support it." And his grand scheme proposes that in the interest of our children we should put the staggering Titan on short commons. Ido not believe that that is a diet which will help that unfortunate person the better to "support the vast orb of his fate." W. V. div.head: [SPECIAL REPORT.]
div.p: [SPECIAL REPORT.]

The Ist V.B. (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment entered on their second week under canvas on Saturday, when they went up the hills and did some hard work in advancing and retiring movements. The work was well carried out, each man acquitting himself creditably, and the morning was well spent. In the afternoon the men were medically inspected by Surgeon-Lieu- tenant Curtis.

On Sunday the whole brigade assembled for a combined church parade in the Welsh Fusiliers lines_; The service was attended by the Governor of the islan (Lord Raglan) and Lady Raglan, Brigadier General H: Hallam Parr (commamfing the North Western districts) and a host of distinguished visitors. The service wag I well carried out and the hearty singing of the men was a treat to hear. At the close of the service, the Welsh Fusiliers sang the Welsh National Anthem in fine style and the old brigade sang "God save the King." The men then marched past ,the general and his staff the general expressing his appreciation at the way the brigade conducted them- selves. An enormous crowd of visitors came into the -catup and saw their friends. In the o-yeuing, numbers of the men left camp for the beautiful glens round Ramsey and Douglas. Some of them had *rip to 'Snaefell's summit in the hope of seeing the four kindoms but on arrival there, they found it was hard work to see four yards, the mist was so thick. About six o'clock rain commenced to fall and It rained incessantly for the rest of the day, spoiling an otherwise nice holiday.

Monday was an important day for the battalion. At eight o'clock, headed by the band, the battalion marched out of camp to Barrule Hill, for a skirmish with the Herefords and Welsh Fusiliers. The •general idea was that a force, consisting of the South Lancashires had effected a landing at Ramsey and were marching to Peel, destroying telegraph wires and signalling station on the way. The action took place at Ballas- hora and lasted , about two hours, the South Lancashires having to retire on their reserves. Return to camp was made about 12.30, everyone being in splen- did appetite. In the afternoon the battalion was inspected in full marching order by the General, who put the maxim gun section and the ambulance section through a, bit of practice. The day was very line, with the exception of a sharp shower about 11 o'clock.

Tuesday's operations were of an interesting nature. It was supposed that a red force based on Laxey had de- tached a force to seize North Barrale. This detached force was supposed to have made a"move on the night of the 3rd. A blue force, consisting of the South Lanes, 10 Mounted Infantry and the Brigade Signallers, were at Lezayre , and unaware of the enemy's move from Laxey had seized North Barrule during the night. The special idea was that the spies had reported that the enemy had moved North from Laxey, but this was unconfirmed. North Barrule must be held at all costs while the main body made a move to Ramsey to embark. A very interesting day was spent and the men made for camp at 2 p.m. In the evening, a lot of fun was caused by the time-honoured game of "blanket- tossing." A number of men were snapshotted up in the air by ardent amateur photograph- ers. A large number of visitors arrived in camp. Oa Wednesday the manoeuvres were on a more exten- sive scale, being taken in conjunction with the line battalions of the Welsh Fusiliers and the North Stfffords, who had encamped at Milntown on Tuesday. The general idea was that a red enemy,consisting of the two line battalions, the Herefordshire Volunteers and the South Lancashire Volunteers, 25Mounted Infantry and 130 cyclists, had arrived from over sea and attacked Douglas and Ramsey. Douglas had held its own, but at Ramsey the attack had been-successful and the reds had landed. The red force now desired to attack Douglas from the north but a blue force based at Peel endeavoured to prevent this. The scouts reported that the Ramsey to Snaefell road was held by the enemy and reds were to advance and clear the road. A very interesting day's work was done, the amateurs being much benefited by their conjunction with the regulars. Major Roome, the former adjutant, arrived in camp on Tuesday and watched the operations with interest, as also did the Rev. W. Bracecamp, who appears to be well enjoying his holiday under canvas.

On Thursday, the operations were again on au exten- sive scale. The battalion marched out of camp at 7.30 and went five miles in the direction of Douglas. The South Lancashires,Cheshires and Herefords opposed the Welsh Fusiliers (volunteersand regulars) and the North ' Staffords (regulars). The day was much marred by a very heavy shower towards 11 o'clock, which wet everyone through. The enemyhad the worst of the wet ag they were in shirt - sleeves. However it was voted on all sides that the day was. well spent and despite the bedraggled condition of the troops, all were in good humour and they gave dinner "sox" at 2 o'clock. Rifles inspection was the order of the afternoon and all enjoyed a well-earned rest Yesterday the First South Lancashire and Second Cheshire Regiments took an active part in the combined operations of the thirtieth brigade with two line battalions. The. South Lancashire Mounted Infantry acted as scouts.. Operations were arduous and over an extensive area gaving rise to long marches. Parading at five, the men left camp at seven, returning quite fresh after six hours' instructive training. The South Lancashiresand Cheshires who have had profitable enjoyable training have won excellent reputation for orderliness and good conduct. Last night concerts and games were indulged in. The battalion start for home at 11 a.m. to-morrow (Sunday) and will probably arrive about 7 o'clock lathe evening. _ _

There are only a few serious cases in the hospital the chief being sprains which are most prevalent among the cyclists. With regard to the cyclists, it may be stated that no fewer thanls "bikes" have been smashed.
FIRST SOUTH LANCASHIRE'S NEW COMMANDER.

The command of the Ist V. 8., the Prince of Wales' Volunteers South Lancashire Regiment, which has beenvaeant for some time, has Row been filled by the promotion of Major J. A. Edelsten a very smart officer with the "Q "certificate who isalso a qualified instruc- tor in army signalling. The new lieutenant-colonel was formerly supply and transport officer to the Volunteer Brigade at Salford. He got his company in 1892, and has been field officer for nearly two years.

CONTRACTORS PINED.

Messrs. Dick, Kerr, and Co., electric tramway con- tractors, who are constructing the joint lines on behalf of the Hyde, Stalybridge, Dukinfield, and Mossley Corporations, were, at Hyde on Thursday, fined 10s. and costs for obstructing the highway in Ashton-road, Newton. THE ALLEGED ASSAULT AT NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS.

At Liverpool Assizes on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Bigham' Thomas Mason (22),labourer, was found not guilty of having assaulted a married woman at Newton-le-Willows, on the 23rd May. His lordship dis- charged prisoner with a caution.

DRUNK. Daniel Conroy was charged at Newton on Monday with having been drunkand disorderly at Earlestown on Sunday. A tine of ss. and costs was imposed.—For having been drunk at Earlestown on Saturday Robert Cardy and George Cornish were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

div.head: SA.D CASE OF ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.
div.p: SA.D CASE OF ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.

A sad case of attempted suicide occupied the atten- tion of the magistrates at the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, when Robert Jones, c9llier, Plank-lane, Leigh, was charged on remand with attempting to commit suicide at New- ton on Sunday.—The evidence showed that on Sunday afternoon, a boy named Reuben Simm saw the prisoner sitting on the bank of the Highfield Moss Pit, Newton, unlacing his boots. Prisoner afterwards entered the water, and when Simm called to him he got hold of the rushes to get out. Simm informed Constable Benson of what had occurred,and the officer met the prisoner, who was wet through, coming away from the pit. Prisoner was taken to Newton Police Station and on being charged with attempting to commit suicide he replied that he was tired of his life and wanted to do away with himself. Prisoner lost his wife a fortnight ago, and she left him with a baby three weeks old. He had since been drinking heavily, although prior to his wife's death he hail not touched drink for three years.—Prisoner now promised never to touch drink again.--Upon prisoner's son undertaking to look after him, the Bench discharged him.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
ACCIDENT AT A PONY-RACE AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Cycle Club sports on Saturday after- noon, a pony-race resulted in a regrettable accident. Mr. T. Lea's Jessie failed to negotiate a corner,ran into the rails, pitched her rider over amongst the spectators, toppled over the rails after him, and rolled upon him. Mr. Lea was picked up unconscious, and conveyed to the cottage hospital. POLICE CHANGES.

Acting-Sergeant Breeze, of the North Wirral Division, has been promoted to the rank of sergeant and transferred to Runcorn, vice Sergeant Bottom, who has retired from the force onaccount of ill-health and has gonelto live near Manchester.P.C.Upton has been trans- ferred from Halton to Sale and his place is taken by P.C. G. H. Walley, of Altrincham. P.C. Proctor,. Preston Brook, has retired on pension' and will be re- placed by P.C. G. %Valley, of the Broxton division. DEATH OF Mn. W. CHADWICK.

The death took place on Saturday night after a long illness, of Mr. William Henry Chadwick, of Leinster gardens, Runcorn. The deceased gentleman, who was in his 70th year, was widely knownand highly esteemed. Me had been manager of the rope manufacturing works at Runcorn Docks under the 4Bridgwater Navigation Co. and the Manchester Ship Canal Co. about 40 years. He was a member of the Bethesda Congregational Church, and had held the principal lay offices. DRUNK AND INCAPABLE.

At the Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. J. Ockleston, Edward John Toole, a sailor, was charged with having been drunk and incapable in Hartley-street, Runcorn, in the small hours of Friday morning. P.C. .Davies proved the case. He said theman arrived in Runcorn at ten o'clock on Thursday night. The captain of the boat told witness that he was drunk then and went ashore and got a bottle of spirits. He was in such a bad state of intoxication that he was unable to appear before a magistrate on Friday morning. A tine of ss. and costs was imposed,

div.head: – DVATH OF A. RUNCORN MANAGER.
div.p: - DVATH OF A. RUNCORN MANAGER.

Mr. William Henry Chadwick, of Lein.ster-gardens, Runcorn, died at a late hour on Saturday night, after a lingering illness. The deceased gentleman had been manager of the rope manufacturing works at Runcorn docks both under the Bridgewater Navigation Company and the Manchester Ship Canal Company for about forty years, and he was widely known and respected. He was a member of the Bethesda Congregational Church, and had held the principal lay offices. He was in his seven- tieth year.

READY FOR WORK IN TWELVE DAYS AFTER NINE MONTHS' SUFFERING. Farfield-street, Bradford, Cleckheaton, February.2so3, 1903. Dear Sir,—l am firmly convinced that there is nothing to equal your Magnetaire treatment for Rheumatism and *Sciatica. I was off work nine months suffering great pain with my back, hip and leg, and part of the time unable to sit in a chair. Seeing a testimonial you have received from the President of the Dewsbury Co-op., I determined to try it, and to my great surprise I was able to dezlare off the club in twelve days and return to work. It was your appliances and nothing else that cleared the Rheumatism out of my system. There is one thing more that I should like you to know, I ant fond of cycling, and during the summer holiday 1 made a big journey to Newcastle, cycling the whole distance, over one hundred miles, in a day. Wishing ylu every success,

There was a sequel to the Rixton poaching affray at the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday when William Green, \Vest Union-street, Salford, was charged with enterinc, land in the occupation of Mr. James Garnett, and taking therefrom two rabbits, on July :20th. Defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. E. A. White, solicitor, prosecuted, and stated that on the night in question, at about eleven o'clock, the defendant was in the wood, accompanied by another mannamed Wilson,who,in trying to escape,wasjdrowned. To some extent the matter had been gone into at the Coroner's inquest, and certain unfounded suggestions were made with reference to the conduct of the game- keepers and Police-Constable Clarke. Although defend- ant now pleaded guilty he (Mr. White) thought it was only fair that the keepers and constable should be called in order to give a correct version of the affair. Defendant stated that he and Wilson entered the wood for the purpose of taking a rabbit. They set two nets, each 50 yards long, and caught two rabbits. Defendant alleged that when the police and gamekeepers came upon the scene, he and Wilson walked quietly towards them for the purpose cf giving themselves up. They were, he said, entirely unarmed and P.C. Clarke and the keepers violently set upon them, savagely illtreated them, and brutally kicked them. On the contrary, the constable and the keepers stated that defendant and Wilson rushed upon them. Defendant aimed a blow at one of the keepers, who, however, dodged the blow and struck defendant on the head with his stick in self-defence. The deceased man struck at the other keeper, but P.C. Clarke interfered and received a blow on the hand. The men then attempted to escape and were chased. Having regard to the fact that Wilson was drowned, the defendant must have suffered a considerable amount of mental anxiety, and he (Mr. White)did not, therefore, wish to press the case unduly. Evidence having been called defendant offered no defence and a fine of 40s. and costs was imposed.

Bank Holiday Railway Traffic. As usual there was heavy railway traffic from War rington to various holiday resorts on Bank ifoliday, the railway companies having made special proyisioll to cope with it. Though unpromising in the early morning the weather during the greater part of the day was beautifully fine, and the trippers thoroughli enjoyed themselves. By the London and North' Western system about 100 inhabitants travelled t°,.. Blackpool on Monday, 300 to North Wales, •80 to Windermere, and 360 to Frodsham. 10 addition there were 200 bookings to Blackpool 01 Saturday and Sunday and 112 to North Wales. The Oheshire Lines trains were exceptionally heavily laden on Monday, 3,000 passengers journeying t° Liverpool and New Brighton, 1,000 to Southport, 2,000 to Manchester awl Belle Vue, and 300 to Derbyshire. During the week-end there were at least 500 bookings to Douglas.
